title: Boundary shape controls the stress distribution in two-component elastic materials
summary: We investigate how the shape and arrangement of high-stiffness regions govern stress redistribution in two-component triangular elastic spring networks subjected to spatially correlated and uncorrelated random prestress. We compare boundary roughness, partitioning into disconnected regions, and graded transitions between regions of different stiffness. Our simulations identify interface bonds as channels for energy transfer: increasing their number provides additional transfer paths and reduces stress concentration in mechanically rigid regimes, while offering little benefit in compliant subnetworks. This is analogous to defects in naturally occurring crystal structures, where the defects themselves isolate stress. At a fixed fraction of high-stiffness material, partitioning reduces stress concentration for both correlated and uncorrelated prestress. The benefit diminishes with further subdivision as the number of interface bonds becomes comparable to the number of interior nodes. Stress reduction, however, depends on the spatial correlations of the imposed prestress: random prestress generally yields a stronger effect, though the difference diminishes in some regimes. Graded interfaces further reduce peak stress by distributing the stiffness transition over a broader region. Together, these results suggest design strategies based on increasing interface area, matching subdivision scale to prestress correlations, and grading stiffness transitions. This minimal framework identifies how internal structure controls energy transfer and stress redistribution, suggesting design principles for mechanical robustness under both internal and external loading.

AI.tldr: By tuning interface length, subdivision scale, and stiffness grading in two-component triangular spring networks, the authors show that interface bonds act as energy-transfer channels whose proliferation reduces peak stress, and that the optimal partitioning scale depends on the correlation length of the imposed prestress.
AI.motivation: Stress concentration in heterogeneous elastic materials is a central failure mechanism, yet it remains unclear how the geometric arrangement of stiff versus compliant regions (roughness, connectivity, grading) controls stress redistribution, particularly when prestress is spatially correlated rather than random. The authors aim for a minimal model that isolates internal structure from material detail.
AI.method: Simulations on two-component triangular elastic spring networks with high- and low-stiffness bonds, loaded by spatially correlated and uncorrelated random prestress. Design variables are (i) boundary roughness of the stiff regions, (ii) partitioning into disconnected stiff regions at fixed stiff-material fraction, and (iii) graded versus sharp stiffness transitions. Metrics focus on peak stress concentration and on interface-bond counts relative to interior-node counts.
AI.result: Interface bonds behave as channels for energy transfer: more interfaces add transfer paths and lower stress concentration in mechanically rigid regimes but give little benefit in compliant subnetworks, echoing defect-mediated stress isolation in crystals. At fixed high-stiffness fraction, partitioning reduces stress concentration for both correlated and uncorrelated prestress, but the gain saturates once interface bonds approach the number of interior nodes. The reduction is stronger for random (uncorrelated) prestress, though the gap narrows in some regimes. Graded interfaces lower peak stress further by spreading the stiffness transition over a broader region.
AI.conclusion: Internal architecture—not just phase fraction—governs energy transfer and stress redistribution. The framework yields three design rules: maximize interface area, match subdivision scale to the prestress correlation length, and grade stiffness transitions. These principles transfer to disordered heterogeneous and architected materials for mechanical robustness under internal and external loading.

title: Existence and Absence of Spin-Glass Phases on Migdal--Kadanoff Hierarchical Lattices: A Complete Classification
summary: We consider the Ising spin-glass model on Migdal--Kadanoff (MK) hierarchical lattices, characterized by the fractal dimension $d=1+\log s/\log b$, where $s$ and $b$ denote the number of parallel branches and the number of bonds in series within each branch, respectively. For independent Gaussian couplings, we rigorously establish a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of finite-temperature spin-glass order for arbitrary integers $b,s\ge2$. We prove that a finite-temperature spin-glass phase exists whenever \[ \frac{b}{\sqrt{s}} \left( \frac{b\sqrt{s(s-1)}}{bs-1} \right)^{s-1}<1. \] In particular, this condition holds for all three-dimensional MK hierarchical lattices ($d=3$, or equivalently $s=b^2$), regardless of the choice of $b$. Conversely, we prove the absence of finite-temperature spin-glass order for fractal dimensions $d<1+\log17/\log6\approx2.58$, as well as in the large-$b$ limit for any fixed $d<3$. In the intermediate regime $1+\log17/\log6\le d<3$, we provide a finite-step procedure to determine the presence or absence of spin-glass order, which depends on $b$ and $s$. Our results provide a complete characterization of finite-temperature spin-glass order on MK hierarchical lattices.

AI.tldr: Rigorous necessary and sufficient condition for finite-temperature spin-glass order in the Ising spin glass on Migdal–Kadanoff hierarchical lattices, for all integers b,s≥2 and Gaussian couplings, fully characterizing the phase diagram in terms of fractal dimension d=1+log s/log b.
AI.motivation: Whether a finite-temperature spin-glass phase exists on hierarchical (Migdal–Kadanoff) lattices with fractal dimension between 2 and 3, and how it depends on the branching geometry, was unresolved; a complete rigorous characterization of the ordering transition for arbitrary b and s was lacking.
AI.method: Recursive (cavity/decimation) analysis of the MK lattice with s parallel branches of b bonds in series, using Gaussian couplings; rigorous bounds and recursion-flow analysis of the spin-glass susceptibility/order parameter to derive an exact existence criterion and a finite-step algorithmic procedure for intermediate dimensions.
AI.result: A finite-temperature spin-glass phase exists iff (b/√s)(b√(s(s−1))/(bs−1))^{s−1} < 1. In particular, order is always present for all d=3 MK lattices (s=b²) for any b. No finite-temperature order occurs for d<1+log17/log6≈2.58 and in the large-b limit for any fixed d<3. For 1+log17/log6≤d<3, a finite-step procedure decides ordering depending on b and s.
AI.conclusion: The paper gives a complete characterization of finite-temperature spin-glass order on MK hierarchical lattices, settling the existence question for arbitrary b,s and delimiting fractal-dimension regimes of guaranteed order, guaranteed disorder, and geometry-dependent behavior.

title: Generalization properties of the token perceptron: the role of embedding and vocabulary
summary: Large language models are trained to predict tokens from a finite vocabulary, each represented by a vector in a $d$-dimensional embedding space. Therefore, token prediction is a classification problem whose classes have a geometry determined by the embedding. We study how this geometry affects learning in a minimal solvable model: a linear predictor that maps a sequence of $N$ embedded tokens to a $d$-dimensional output through one $d\times d$ matrix per position, trained in the teacher--student setting. We call this the \textit{token perceptron}. We compute its generalization error with the replica method, taking $N\to\infty$ at fixed number of examples per position $α=P/N$ and keeping $d$ and the vocabulary size $D$ finite. As a first reference case, we consider continuous embeddings on the sphere, which isolate the role of the embedding dimension. The natural load is then $α/d$, and for $d>1$ a normalized label fixes the direction of the teacher output, so the problem becomes a noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above $α_{\rm rec}=d^2/(d-1)$, and spherical cross-entropy reaches this threshold at large inverse temperature. In the same setting the storage capacity of random associations scales as $d^2$ for margins $O(1/\sqrt{d})$. We then turn to vocabulary embeddings, where a label only identifies the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, so that each example imposes inequalities rather than equations, as in the classical perceptron. We compute the Bayes-optimal error for a given embedding matrix through an approximate spectral closure and show that the optimal learner first resolves the directions in which the vocabulary has the largest variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.

AI.tldr: A "token perceptron"—a linear predictor mapping N embedded tokens to a d-dim output via per-position matrices—is solved in the teacher-student setting with the replica method. For spherical embeddings, token prediction reduces to noiseless regression, with exact teacher recovery above α_rec = d²/(d−1); for realistic vocabulary embeddings, labels only constrain Voronoi cells (inequalities), and the Bayes-optimal learner resolves highest-variance vocabulary directions first.
AI.motivation: Token prediction is fundamentally a classification problem over a finite vocabulary whose class geometry is fixed by the embedding vectors. Prior work has not isolated how this embedding geometry shapes learning. This paper builds a minimal solvable model to disentangle the role of embedding dimension and vocabulary structure.
AI.method: The authors study the "token perceptron": a linear predictor mapping a sequence of N embedded tokens to a d-dimensional output through one d×d matrix per position, trained in a teacher-student setting. Generalization error is computed with the replica method, taking N→∞ at fixed examples-per-position α=P/N while keeping d and vocabulary size D finite. Two cases are analyzed: (1) continuous spherical embeddings isolating embedding-dimension effects, where the natural load is α/d; and (2) general vocabulary embeddings, where labels only identify the Voronoi cell of the teacher output, yielding inequality constraints (perceptron-like), solved via an approximate spectral closure for the Bayes-optimal error.
AI.result: For spherical embeddings with d>1, a normalized label fixes the teacher output direction, making the problem noiseless regression: the teacher is recovered exactly above α_rec = d²/(d−1), and spherical cross-entropy attains this threshold at large inverse temperature. Storage capacity of random associations scales as d² for margins O(1/√d). For vocabulary embeddings, the Bayes-optimal error is computed for a given embedding matrix, showing the optimal learner first resolves directions of largest vocabulary variance, even when the teacher is isotropic.
AI.conclusion: Embedding geometry critically governs learning in token prediction. Spherical continuous embeddings yield a sharp noiseless-regression recovery threshold and d²-capacity scaling, while finite-vocabulary embeddings impose inequality constraints that induce a spectral, variance-prioritized learning order—revealing how vocabulary structure steers the optimization independently of teacher isotropy.

title: Verified Pauli-Product Measurement Compilation for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation
summary:
Fault-tolerant quantum compilers implement gates through Pauli-product measurements and classical feedback. Verifying such a compiler requires reasoning about the quantum state and the recorded outcomes together: a correction reads an outcome, a gate's internal outcomes must be hidden from its caller, and an application's outcomes must survive optimization. We introduce QPPM, a language for Pauli-product measurement programs, with a weakest-precondition semantics over store-indexed matrix assertions, following quantum Hoare logic with classical variables. Every program terminates, so the Hoare logic is a syntactic presentation of weakest preconditions whose soundness and relative completeness are immediate. Its value is that component specifications compose. All results are mechanized in Lean.
  We verify lowering of Clifford+$T$ circuits to QPPM with private outcomes and supplied magic states, and an optimizer that eliminates measurements, fuses and reorders rotations, and schedules logical rounds while preserving every outcome that subsequent code can read. A compositional approximation relation bounds the effect of synthesis error on specifications and on output trace distance, and a certificate-checked pipeline selects, among synthesized circuits that meet the user's error limit, the one with the lowest certified depth bound. On QASMBench, verified fusion and scheduling reduce logical measurement depth by a median of 17.9\%, and complete source-to-QPPM allowances are certified for all 35 valid selected small-suite inputs.

AI.tldr: QPPM is a language for fault-tolerant Pauli-product measurement programs with a weakest-precondition semantics over store-indexed matrix assertions, enabling compositional verification of quantum compilers. All results are mechanized in Lean, including verification of Clifford+T lowering and an outcome-preserving optimizer that reduces logical measurement depth by a median of 17.9% on QASMBench.
AI.motivation: Fault-tolerant compilers implement gates via Pauli-product measurements and classical feedback, so verifying them requires joint reasoning about quantum state and recorded outcomes. Key challenges include corrections reading outcomes, hiding a gate's internal outcomes from its caller, and preserving application outcomes across optimization—a compositional specification framework is needed.
AI.method: Introduces QPPM, a language for Pauli-product measurement programs, with a weakest-precondition semantics over store-indexed matrix assertions following quantum Hoare logic with classical variables. Programs always terminate, making the Hoare logic a syntactic presentation of weakest preconditions with immediate soundness and relative completeness. Uses compositional specifications, a compositional approximation relation bounding synthesis error effects on specifications and output trace distance, and a certificate-checked pipeline selecting the lowest certified depth bound among error-compliant circuits. Mechanized in Lean.
AI.result: Verifies Clifford+T lowering to QPPM with private outcomes and supplied magic states, plus an optimizer eliminating measurements, fusing/reordering rotations, and scheduling logical rounds while preserving readable outcomes. On QASMBench, verified fusion and scheduling reduce logical measurement depth by a median of 17.9%; complete source-to-QPPM allowances are certified for all 35 valid selected small-suite inputs.
AI.conclusion: QPPM provides a principled, compositional, fully mechanized framework for verifying fault-tolerant quantum compilers, demonstrating that verified optimization passes yield real depth reductions while preserving outcome semantics and certifying error bounds end-to-end.

title: Mutual Information Across Quantum Reference Frame Perspectives
summary: In quantum information theory, standard notions typically presuppose a fixed partition of the world into subsystems, encoded in a tensor product structure of the Hilbert space. Yet, in some scenarios, the subsystem structure is not uniquely fixed. A case in point is the description of subsystems relative to different quantum reference frames (QRFs), where the tensor product structure, although fixed in a specific QRF, changes across different QRFs. Such a relativity of subsystems underlies many interesting features of QRFs, such as the relativity of entanglement, entropy, and coherence. It also raises a broader question: how do we compare the information across different subsystem perspectives, especially when the corresponding subsystem algebras overlap? Here, we propose a notion of quantum mutual information across different QRF perspectives, which captures the correlations between subsystems relative to different frames of reference. To do so, we focus on an algebraic definition of subsystems. Studying in detail the union and overlap between subsystem algebras relative to different QRFs, we find that the usual definition of mutual information in terms of the chain law overcounts the information associated to the overlap. Based on this insight, we propose a modified chain law and show that the resulting notion of mutual information satisfies subadditivity and connects naturally to other measures found in the literature [1]. Our investigations not only provide a way to quantify the relation between different QRF perspectives from an information-theoretic point of view but also sheds light on some important features of quantum information in absence of a fixed tensor product structure.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a frame-relative notion of quantum mutual information by using an algebraic definition of subsystems across different quantum reference frames (QRFs), correcting the overcounting in the standard chain-law definition when subsystem algebras overlap.
AI.motivation: Standard quantum information presupposes a fixed subsystem partition encoded in a tensor product structure. Under QRFs this structure changes between frames, making entanglement, entropy, and coherence frame-relative. A key open question is how to compare information across different QRF perspectives, especially when the corresponding subsystem algebras overlap, since the usual chain-law mutual information overcounts the overlap contribution.
AI.method: Adopt an algebraic definition of subsystems and analyze the union and overlap of subsystem algebras relative to different QRFs. Show that the standard chain-law decomposition of mutual information overcounts information associated with the algebraic overlap, then propose a modified chain law for mutual information across QRF perspectives.
AI.result: The modified mutual information satisfies subadditivity and connects naturally to other measures in the literature. It provides a quantitative information-theoretic characterization of the relation between different QRF perspectives.
AI.conclusion: The work offers a way to quantify correlations between subsystems relative to different reference frames and clarifies features of quantum information when no fixed tensor product structure exists.

title: The Entire Quantum Computer on a Classical Leash
summary:
We show that a classical client with no quantum hardware can use a single untrusted and potentially malicious quantum server as if it were its own trusted quantum computer. Through the server, the client can privately choose and run quantum computations, prepare quantum states, and process quantum states supplied by other parties. It can also keep quantum memory on the server, hidden from the server itself, and use that memory in later computations so its quantum state persists across rounds of interaction. Together, these capabilities let a purely classical party act as a quantum party in a variety of interactive protocols.
  We expect this virtual quantum computer to be a broadly useful tool. As immediate applications, we resolve two known open problems: (1) classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error, and (2) remote state preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable quantum states.
  Underlying all of these results is a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol between a classical client and a quantum server, which we construct assuming only the post-quantum hardness of learning with errors.

AI.tldr: A purely classical client can use one untrusted quantum server as its own trusted quantum computer via a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol based only on post-quantum LWE hardness, yielding hidden quantum memory, private quantum computation, and two open-problem solutions.
AI.motivation: Classical parties lack quantum hardware but want to act as full quantum parties in interactive protocols. Prior work did not give a classical client the ability to privately compute, store, and reuse quantum states on a single untrusted server with malicious security under standard assumptions.
AI.method: Construct a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol between a classical client and a quantum server, assuming only the post-quantum hardness of learning with errors (LWE). This protocol underlies a "virtual quantum computer" enabling private quantum computation, state preparation, processing of externally supplied states, and persistent hidden quantum memory across rounds.
AI.result: Achieves a classical client acting as a quantum party: private choice and execution of quantum computations, quantum state preparation, processing of states from other parties, and server-hidden persistent quantum memory. Resolves two open problems: (1) classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error, and (2) remote state preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable quantum states.
AI.conclusion: A classical client can securely outsource full quantum capabilities to a single untrusted quantum server, establishing a broadly useful virtual quantum computer from post-quantum LWE alone.

title: Quantum Complexity and Stabilizer-State Expansions: From Pairing to Deformation in Fermionic Systems
summary: Understanding how collective phenomena such as pairing and deformation emerge in interacting fermionic systems, and how the correlations underlying them shape the resources required for their simulation, is a central challenge in many-body physics. We investigate various aspects of quantum complexity in a fermionic system exhibiting two main forms of collectivity, specifically deformation and pairing, through entanglement, non-stabilizerness, and fermionic non-Gaussianity. In the deformed phase, high entanglement coexists with low non-stabilizerness, while the superfluid pairing phase, by contrast, exhibits substantial multipartite entanglement and non-stabilizerness, together with maximal fermionic anti-flatness. In a second step we examine how to describe the phase diagram of the system in a classically scalable and symmetry-preserving way, by combining stabilizer-state expansion and variational basis optimization. A physics-guided decomposition of the Hamiltonian identifies the relevant stabilizer states, which can be constructed from graph states. A single stabilizer state captures the deformed phase to a large extent, and, although the number of stabilizer states required to describe the pairing phase grows exponentially with system size, a symmetry-preserving basis rotation yields a high-fidelity approximation using far fewer states. This rotated state can then serve as a practical starting point for quantum refinement.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes quantum complexity in a fermionic system featuring deformation and pairing collectivity via entanglement, non-stabilizerness, and fermionic non-Gaussianity, then proposes a classically scalable, symmetry-preserving stabilizer-state-expansion plus variational-basis-optimization framework (with basis rotations) to capture the phase diagram.
AI.motivation: To understand how collective phenomena (pairing, deformation) emerge in interacting fermionic systems and how the correlations underlying them dictate simulation resources, and to find a scalable, symmetry-preserving way to describe the phase diagram.
AI.method: Characterizes quantum complexity through entanglement, non-stabilizerness (magic), and fermionic non-Gaussianity (anti-flatness); then describes the phase diagram classically using stabilizer-state expansion combined with variational basis optimization, where a physics-guided Hamiltonian decomposition identifies relevant stabilizer states constructible from graph states, plus a symmetry-preserving basis rotation.
AI.result: Deformed phase shows high entanglement coexisting with low non-stabilizerness; superfluid pairing phase shows substantial multipartite entanglement and non-stabilizerness with maximal fermionic anti-flatness. A single stabilizer state largely captures the deformed phase; the number of stabilizer states needed for the pairing phase grows exponentially with system size, but a symmetry-preserving basis rotation achieves high fidelity with far fewer states.
AI.conclusion: Distinct collective phases exhibit distinct complexity signatures, and stabilizer-state expansion with symmetry-preserving basis rotation provides a classically scalable, high-fidelity description whose rotated state serves as a practical starting point for quantum refinement.

title: Temporal Degeneracy Limits Message Passing Decoding of QLDPC Codes Under Repeated Noisy Syndrome Measurements
summary: Practical quantum computations can require logical error rates of $10^{-12}$ or lower. Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are promising candidates for reaching such rates with low qubit overhead, provided that their syndromes can be decoded efficiently. Repeated noisy syndrome measurements introduce temporal degeneracy into the space-time decoding graph. We characterize the temporal kernel, whose vectors have zero total data parity, and show that it is generated by elementary temporal codewords of weight $d_v+2$, where $d_v$ is the variable-node degree. For $(d_v,d_c)$-regular parity-check matrices with fixed degrees $d_v,d_c>2$ and girth greater than four, we derive counting bounds and construct degenerate error patterns of weight $(d_v+2)/2$ for even $d_v$ and $d_v+1$ for odd $d_v$, with multiplicity $Θ(nr)$ in the blocklength $n$ and number of measurement rounds $r$. Under the isolation assumption, these patterns cause local failures of deterministic isotropic message-passing decoders under a flooding schedule. These failures depend on the node degrees rather than the minimum distance; for the bivariate bicycle (BB) codes considered, their weight is equal to four. Monte carlo simulations and fixed-weight importance sampling quantify harmful low-weight degenerate error patterns for the min-sum (MS) decoder beyond the isolation assumption. Motivated by the identified symmetries, we propose space-time anisotropic min-sum decoding with syndrome-guided realizations. Its complexity is linear in the number of Tanner graph edges for fixed maximum number of iterations and number of decoders. Numerical results on BB codes show threshold-like behavior acrossthe tested code sizes and improved failure probabilities relative to MS decoding with ordered statistics decoding post-processing.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes the temporal kernel of the space-time decoding graph for noisy-syndrome QLDPC decoding, proves the existence of numerous low-weight degenerate error patterns (weight ~4 for bivariate bicycle codes) that trap deterministic isotropic message-passing decoders, and proposes a space-time anisotropic min-sum decoder with syndrome-guided realizations that improves failure probability at linear complexity.
AI.motivation: Practical quantum computation needs logical error rates ≤10^-12, and QLDPC codes can reach this with low qubit overhead only if syndromes are decoded efficiently. Repeated noisy syndrome measurements create temporal degeneracy in the space-time decoding graph, but the structure of this degeneracy and its effect on message-passing decoders is not well understood; the paper aims to characterize it and exploit the insight to build a better decoder.
AI.method: Defines and characterizes the temporal kernel (vectors with zero total data parity), showing it is generated by elementary temporal codewords of weight d_v+2. For (d_v,d_c)-regular parity-check matrices with degrees >2 and girth >4, derives counting bounds and explicitly constructs degenerate error patterns of weight (d_v+2)/2 (even d_v) or d_v+1 (odd d_v) with multiplicity Θ(nr). Uses Monte Carlo simulations and fixed-weight importance sampling to quantify harmful low-weight degenerate patterns for MS decoding beyond the isolation assumption, then designs a space-time anisotropic min-sum decoder with syndrome-guided realizations.
AI.result: Under the isolation assumption, the constructed degenerate patterns cause local failures of deterministic isotropic message-passing decoders under flooding scheduling; these failures depend on node degrees rather than minimum distance, and for BB codes the harmful weight equals four. Simulation and importance sampling confirm harmful low-weight degenerate patterns for MS decoding. The proposed anisotropic min-sum decoder has complexity linear in the number of Tanner graph edges (for fixed max iterations and number of decoders), shows threshold-like behavior across tested BB code sizes, and yields improved failure probabilities compared with MS decoding plus ordered-statistics-decoding post-processing.
AI.conclusion: Temporal degeneracy in the space-time decoding graph yields abundant low-weight degenerate patterns that trap standard isotropic decoders independent of code distance. Exploiting the identified symmetries through space-time anisotropic min-sum decoding with syndrome-guided realizations provides a low-complexity, linear-time decoder that improves failure probability on BB codes, indicating it is a practical route toward the very low logical error rates required for quantum computation.

title: Optimal Control of a Fluxonium Circuit with the Q-PRONTO Numerical Method
summary: Optimizing the control of large quantum systems is a resource-intensive task, where the convergence rate of the underlying iterative schemes is crucial. The recently developed Quantum Projection Operator-Based Newton Method for Trajectory Optimization (Q-PRONTO) offers a unique quadratic convergence for controlling quantum states, while most model-based solvers guarantee only an approximately linear convergence rate. As a proof of concept, here, we design and benchmark single-qubit gates optimized by Q-PRONTO based on the circuit Hamiltonian of a fluxonium superconducting qubit. To ensure that we can apply a long string of arbitrary pulses to the circuit, we modify the firmware associated with the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) by altering its memory allocation. We characterize the performance of the optimal solutions using standard randomized benchmarking and achieve a total error per gate of $6.6\times10^{-4}$.

AI.tldr: Q-PRONTO enables quadratic-convergence quantum optimal control; here it is benchmarked by optimizing single-qubit fluxonium gates with modified QICK firmware, achieving 6.6e-4 error per gate.
AI.motivation: Controlling large quantum systems is resource-intensive, and convergence rate of iterative optimal-control solvers is critical. Most model-based solvers guarantee only approximately linear convergence, while Q-PRONTO offers quadratic convergence; this work provides a proof-of-concept experimental benchmark.
AI.method: Single-qubit gates were optimized with Q-PRONTO using the circuit Hamiltonian of a fluxonium superconducting qubit. The QICK firmware was modified (memory allocation) to allow long strings of arbitrary pulses to be applied. Performance was characterized via standard randomized benchmarking.
AI.result: A total error per gate of 6.6e-4 was achieved with Q-PRONTO-optimized single-qubit fluxonium gates.
AI.conclusion: Q-PRONTO's quadratic-convergence trajectory optimization is experimentally viable for pulse-level quantum control, yielding low per-gate error; firmware-level modifications enable practical pulse delivery.

title: Graphical Rigidity of Continuous Variable Graph States under Gaussian Local Transformations
summary: Multimode entangled pure Gaussian states are an essential resource for continuous variable (CV) quantum information processing. Menicucci et al. [2011] have shown how to describe them as graphs with complex adjacency matrices. Among such complex graph states (CGSs), quantum optics experimental setups straightforwardly display correlations described by purely imaginary graph states (iRGSs) whereas theoretical literature favors off-diagonal real graph state (RGS) descriptions, which actually reflect the entanglement structure in the infinite squeezing limit [Gonzalez-Arciniegas et al. 2021]. We study them beyond this ideal case, thus establishing in the finite squeezing regime an equivalence criterion for the generic case of CGSs through a graph propagating set of conditions which either finds a Gaussian Local Unitary (GLU) converting one state to another or gives a proof of impossibility if such a GLU does not exist. In the experimentally relevant case of the conversion between iRGSs and RGSs, the set of conditions results in simple relations between the topologies of the equivalent real and imaginary graphs. Finally, we show that the canonical forms of iRGSs and RGSs imply that the topology of the CV real and imaginary graph states are too rigid to admit any exact qumode local-addition analogue to the qubit complementation or qudit local-addition, thus demonstrating the non-existence of any exact qumode local-addition for these states. We however define an approximate one when the squeezing is strong enough.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a finite-squeezing equivalence criterion for complex Gaussian graph states via graph-propagating conditions, derives simple topological relations for converting imaginary graph states to real graph states, and proves that no exact qumode local-addition analogue to qubit complementation exists, while proposing an approximate version valid at strong squeezing.
AI.motivation: Multimode entangled pure Gaussian states are key resources for CV quantum information, described as complex-adjacency graph states. Experimentally, setups naturally yield purely imaginary graph states (iRGSs), while theory prefers off-diagonal real graph states (RGSs) reflecting entanglement structure only in the infinite-squeezing limit. A rigorous equivalence theory beyond this idealization is missing.
AI.method: The authors study complex graph states in the finite-squeezing regime and construct a graph-propagating set of conditions that either yields a Gaussian Local Unitary (GLU) mapping one CGS to another or proves impossibility. For the iRGS–RGS conversion, these conditions reduce to simple relations between the topologies of the equivalent real and imaginary graphs; canonical forms of iRGSs and RGSs are used to test local-addition operations.
AI.result: The criterion decides GLU equivalence of generic CGSs at finite squeezing. For iRGS↔RGS conversion it gives simple topology relations between the equivalent graphs. The canonical forms show that CV real and imaginary graph-state topologies are too rigid to admit any exact qumode local-addition analogue of qubit complementation or qudit local-addition, proving non-existence of such exact operations; an approximate local-addition is defined for sufficiently strong squeezing.
AI.conclusion: GLU equivalence of entangled pure Gaussian graph states can be decided constructively at finite squeezing, iRGSs and RGSs are related by simple graph-topology rules, and exact qumode local-addition does not exist for these states, though a strong-squeezing approximation is available.

title: Fidelity Dynamics of a Jaynes--Cummings Qubit under Markovian and Non-Markovian Coupling Noise
summary: We analytically investigate the fidelity dynamics of a Jaynes--Cummings qubit coupled to a single-mode cavity in the presence of stochastic fluctuations of the qubit--cavity coupling. Such fluctuations naturally arise in cavity- and circuit-QED platforms due to fabrication imperfections, control-field noise, mechanical vibrations, and environmental disturbances. Since the qubit--cavity coupling governs the rate of coherent energy and information exchange, understanding the effects of its fluctuations is essential for assessing the performance of quantum communication, quantum sensing, and quantum information-processing protocols. We consider both Gaussian white noise and Ornstein--Uhlenbeck noise with finite correlation time as models for the coupling fluctuations. Exploiting the closed dynamics within each excitation manifold, we derive exact analytical expressions for the noise-averaged density matrix and the fidelity relative to the ideal noiseless evolution. We show that the fidelity is determined by a single decoherence factor governed by the integrated noise correlation function, establishing a direct connection between microscopic coupling fluctuations and macroscopic coherence loss. In the white-noise limit, the fidelity decays exponentially, whereas finite noise correlation times produce nonexponential decay and slower coherence loss. We further show that the crossover between Markovian-like and non-Markovian regimes is controlled by the ratio of the noise correlation rate to the coherent coupling strength, and that decoherence increases with photon number because of the enhanced effective qubit--cavity coupling. These results provide a unified analytical framework for quantifying decoherence induced by stochastic coupling fluctuations and for evaluating the robustness of cavity-QED protocols under correlated noise.

AI.tldr: Exact analytical treatment of fidelity loss in a Jaynes–Cummings qubit under stochastic fluctuations of the qubit–cavity coupling, with Gaussian white and Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noise models, showing fidelity collapse is governed by a single decoherence factor.
AI.motivation: Qubit–cavity coupling fluctuations arise inevitably in cavity- and circuit-QED from fabrication imperfections, control noise, mechanical vibrations, and environmental disturbance. Since the coupling sets the rate of coherent energy/information exchange, quantifying how its fluctuations degrade coherence is needed to assess quantum communication, sensing, and information-processing protocols.
AI.method: Model coupling fluctuations as Gaussian white noise and as Ornstein–Uhlenbeck noise with finite correlation time. Exploit the closed dynamics within each excitation manifold to derive exact analytical expressions for the noise-averaged density matrix and the fidelity relative to the ideal noiseless evolution.
AI.result: Fidelity is set by a single decoherence factor governed by the integrated noise correlation function, linking microscopic coupling fluctuations to macroscopic coherence loss. White noise gives exponential decay; finite correlation time yields nonexponential decay with slower decoherence. The Markovian-to-non-Markovian crossover is controlled by the ratio of the noise correlation rate to the coherent coupling strength, and decoherence increases with photon number due to enhanced effective coupling.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified analytical framework for quantifying decoherence from stochastic coupling fluctuations and for evaluating the robustness of cavity-QED protocols under correlated noise.

title: Noise-Assisted Quantum Entanglement: Memory-Enhanced Coherence in Stochastic Jaynes-Cummings Dynamics
summary: We investigate qubit entanglement dynamics in a two-qubit cavity system with stochastically fluctuating coupling strength, comparing white noise (Markovian) and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise (non-Markovian) processes. We analytically solve the system dynamics for both Fock and coherent cavity states and systematically characterize how initial qubit configurations affect entanglement generation and preservation. Our results reveal distinct dynamical regimes: in the Fock-state cavity, initial states in the single-excitation subspace generate robust qubit entanglement in decoherence-free subspaces, while initially entangled states in the double-excitation subspace exhibit inevitable decay without protective symmetries. For coherent cavities, we identify a critical photon-number threshold in the intermediate coherent-state amplitude regime where dynamics transition from low-frequency to high-frequency entanglement oscillations, while universal entanglement loss occurs at large amplitudes. Remarkable resilience against entanglement sudden death emerges under strong non-Markovian noise with long correlation times, where repeated revivals occur. These findings establish cavity photon statistics and environmental memory time as key control parameters for engineering qubit entanglement dynamics in qubit-cavity systems, revealing how system-environment correlations govern quantum information preservation.

AI.tldr: Entanglement dynamics of two qubits coupled to a noisy cavity is solved analytically for white vs. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise, identifying Fock/coherent photon statistics and environmental memory time as key control knobs.
AI.motivation: Qubit-cavity platforms are central to quantum information, but how stochastic coupling fluctuations (with different noise memory) and cavity photon statistics jointly govern entanglement generation and preservation is not systematically understood.
AI.method: Analytical solution of two-qubit entanglement dynamics in a cavity with stochastically fluctuating coupling, comparing white (Markovian) and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (non-Markovian) noise, for both Fock and coherent cavity states; systematic scan over initial qubit configurations (single- vs. double-excitation subspaces, initial entangled vs. separable states).
AI.result: Fock cavity: single-excitation initial states yield robust entanglement in decoherence-free subspaces, while double-excitation entangled states decay inexorably absent symmetry protection. Coherent cavity: a critical photon-number threshold in the intermediate-amplitude regime separates low- from high-frequency entanglement oscillations, with universal entanglement loss at large amplitudes. Strong non-Markovian noise with long correlation times enables revivals and suppresses entanglement sudden death.
AI.conclusion: Cavity photon statistics and environmental memory time act as primary control parameters for engineering entanglement in qubit-cavity systems; system-environment correlations determine quantum information preservation.

title: Demonstrating RFSoC-based Control of a Fully Connected Exchange-Only Qubit
summary: Semiconductor triple-quantum dots (TQDs) are a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, but the community has so far lacked access to affordable and flexible high-speed control electronics. SpinQICK, an open-source spin qubit-control package built on the Xilinx Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC), directly addresses this gap by leveraging the high sampling-rate signal generation and advanced digital signal processing (DSP) capabilities of the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) to enable precise time-domain voltage control and readout of semiconductor spin qubits. In this paper, we use spinQICK to demonstrate coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only device. We also introduce and experimentally verify a novel dynamical decoupling (DD) sequence enabled by the triangular TQD and leverage its unique decoupling properties to characterize electrical noise. These results establish spinQICK as a low-cost, flexible platform for semiconductor spin qubit control and provide a pathway for hardware optimization through qubit-level noise diagnostics.

AI.tldr: SpinQICK, an open-source RFSoC-based spin qubit control package, is demonstrated on a triangular exchange-only triple-quantum-dot device for coherent control, state preparation, and readout, and used with a novel dynamical decoupling sequence to diagnose electrical noise.
AI.motivation: Semiconductor triple-quantum dots are a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, yet the community lacks affordable, flexible high-speed control electronics. This work aims to close that instrumentation gap.
AI.method: The authors build spinQICK on the Xilinx RFSoC, reusing the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK)'s high-sampling-rate signal generation and DSP to provide precise time-domain voltage control and readout of spin qubits. They use it to perform coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only TQD, and introduce a new dynamical decoupling sequence native to the triangular geometry, applying its decoupling properties to characterize electrical noise.
AI.result: Coherent control, state preparation, and readout are experimentally demonstrated on the triangular exchange-only device. The novel DD sequence is experimentally verified and shown to yield unique decoupling properties that enable extraction of electrical noise characteristics.
AI.conclusion: SpinQICK is established as a low-cost, flexible platform for semiconductor spin qubit control, and qubit-level noise diagnostics via the triangular TQD's DD sequence offer a pathway toward hardware optimization.

title: QuantumMatterExplorer: An Autonomous Agent for the Discovery of Quantum Many-Body Phases of Matter
comment: 42 pages, 10 figures and 3 tables in the main manuscript. Includes a 13-page agent-generated research note
summary: Mapping the phase diagram of a new quantum Hamiltonian demands expert judgement at every step: which observables to measure, where in parameter space to compute, or how to separate genuine order from finite-size artefacts. We introduce QuantumMatterExplorer, an autonomous agent that takes only a Hamiltonian and its parameter ranges as input and returns a phase diagram obtained from its own numerical simulations. The agent is built on a large language model and is designed to reason over a long horizon, maintain a persistent written plan, and drive a set of computational tools, with density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations cross-checked against independent exact diagonalization. The agent combines a large language model with persistent planning, a library of expert computational-physics skills, and density-matrix renormalization group calculations validated against independent exact diagonalization. It adaptively selects quantities to evaluate, refines parameter scans, and performs finite-size analyses as evidence accumulates. After validating the approach on Hamiltonians with known transitions, we challenge it with a frustrated bilinear-biquadratic spin-1 chain with single-ion anisotropy, whose two-dimensional phase diagram was published only recently and is unlikely to appear in any training corpus. Given no hint about the expected physics, the agent proposes which observables to probe, and identifies candidate Néel, Haldane and dimerized phases, in broad agreement with the reference phase diagram. It also detects incommensurate correlations and infers the frustration-dependent geometry of the phase boundaries, all within an eight-hour compute budget. These results open a practical route to the autonomous computational discovery of new phases of quantum matter.

AI.tldr: QuantumMatterExplorer is an LLM-based autonomous agent that, given only a Hamiltonian and its parameter ranges, plans and runs DMRG simulations (cross-checked by exact diagonalization) to produce a phase diagram, and it recovers the known Néel, Haldane and dimerized phases of a frustrated spin-1 chain with single-ion anisotropy.
AI.motivation: Mapping phase diagrams of new quantum Hamiltonians requires continuous expert judgement—choosing observables, deciding where to sample parameter space, and distinguishing genuine order from finite-size artefacts. This motivates automating the workflow to enable autonomous computational discovery of new phases of quantum matter.
AI.method: The agent is built on a large language model with persistent written planning over a long horizon and drives a library of expert computational-physics skills. Core numerics are density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations validated against independent exact diagonalization. It adaptively selects observables, refines parameter scans, and performs finite-size analyses as evidence accumulates.
AI.result: Validated on Hamiltonians with known transitions, then tested on a frustrated bilinear-biquadratic spin-1 chain with single-ion anisotropy whose 2D phase diagram was only recently published. With no hints, the agent proposed observables and identified candidate Néel, Haldane and dimerized phases in broad agreement with the reference diagram, detected incommensurate correlations, and inferred the frustration-dependent geometry of phase boundaries within an eight-hour compute budget.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates a practical route to autonomous computational discovery of new phases of quantum matter using LLM-driven agents with validated tensor-network numerics.

title: Additive uncertainty relations via pseudospectral methods
summary: Given Hermitian observable $A$, the variance of $A$ is given by the difference of expectations $\langle A^2\rangle - \langle A\rangle^2$, where the expectation of an observable implicitly assumes a choice of state for the underlying system. As a sub-case of a general lower bound for the sum of variances for finitely many arbitrary elements in a $C^*$-algebra, we prove that the sum of the variances for $d$ observables $A_1, \dots , A_d$ is greater than some expression in the expectations $\langle i[A_j,A_k]\rangle$ for $j\neq k$ plus the square of the smallest singular value of the associated localizer. In special cases, this expression is just a root mean square average. Our technique also derives a general containment between the Clifford pseudospectra and quadratic pseudospectra for $d$ observables.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a lower bound on the sum of variances of finitely many Hermitian elements of a $C^*$-algebra, expressed via commutator expectations plus the squared smallest singular value of a localizer, and derives containment relations between Clifford and quadratic pseudospectra.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty relations constrain how precisely observables can be jointly determined; the authors seek a general, algebra-level variance-sum lower bound that unifies known uncertainty inequalities and connects them to pseudospectral geometry.
AI.method: A general lower bound for the sum of variances of finitely many arbitrary elements in a $C^*$-algebra is established, specialized to $d$ Hermitian observables to yield a bound in terms of the expectations $\langle i[A_j,A_k]\rangle$ for $j\neq k$ plus the square of the smallest singular value of the associated localizer; the same technique yields a containment between Clifford pseudospectra and quadratic pseudospectra.
AI.result: The variance sum of $d$ observables is bounded below by an expression in the commutator expectations plus the squared smallest singular value of the localizer; in special cases this reduces to a root mean square average, and a general containment of Clifford pseudospectra within quadratic pseudospectra for $d$ observables is obtained.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a unified $C^*$-algebraic lower bound for sums of variances, recovering familiar uncertainty relations as special cases, and links uncertainty quantification to pseudospectral inclusion results.

title: Asymptotic scars arising from the remnants of quantum phase transitions
summary: Many-body localisation, Hilbert space fragmentation and quantum many-body scars (QMBS) are well-established mechanisms of ergodicity breaking in quantum systems. Recently, asymptotic quantum many-body scars (AQMBS), non-thermal states whose stability grows with system size, have been proposed theoretically and probed experimentally. Here, we show that AQMBS arise naturally as remnants of certain quantum phase transitions. For a broad class of frustration-free Hamiltonians, we prove that their gapless excitations survive deformation into a scarred Hamiltonian as states whose energy variance is bounded by the excitation gap. Consequently, the gapless excitations at a quantum critical point become AQMBS of the scarred Hamiltonian. Their fidelity relaxation time is then set by the critical scaling of the gap, determined by the dynamic critical exponent. Modelling the critical Fredkin and Motzkin chains and the two-dimensional PVBS model, we obtain AQMBS whose variances directly reflect the dynamic exponents of the underlying transitions. Where the gap of the Motzkin chain closes super-exponentially, we find exponentially stable AQMBS, for which we also observe numerical evidence of volume-law entanglement.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that asymptotic quantum many-body scars (AQMBS) arise as remnants of quantum phase transitions in frustration-free Hamiltonians, where critical gapless excitations persist under scarring deformation with variance bounded by the excitation gap, and demonstrates this on the critical Fredkin, Motzkin, and 2D PVBS models.
AI.motivation: AQMBS (non-thermal states whose stability grows with system size) were recently proposed and experimentally probed, but a systematic origin for them was lacking. The authors aim to connect ergodicity-breaking scar states to quantum phase transitions, showing AQMBS emerge naturally as remnants of criticality.
AI.method: For a broad class of frustration-free Hamiltonians, they analytically prove that gapless excitations survive deformation into a scarred Hamiltonian as states whose energy variance is bounded by the excitation gap; at a critical point, these gapless excitations become AQMBS. The fidelity relaxation time is then governed by critical scaling of the gap via the dynamic critical exponent. They model the critical Fredkin and Motzkin chains and the 2D PVBS model to test the framework.
AI.result: The constructed AQMBS have variances that directly reflect the dynamic exponents of the underlying transitions. For the Motzkin chain, whose gap closes super-exponentially, they find exponentially stable AQMBS, and also observe numerical evidence of volume-law entanglement for these states.
AI.conclusion: AQMBS naturally emerge as remnants of quantum phase transitions in frustration-free Hamiltonians, with their stability quantitatively linked to the dynamic critical exponent. This provides a unifying mechanism for asymptotic scarring and predicts unusually stable, volume-law-entangled scar states in models with super-exponential gap closing.

title: Robustness of Quantum Correlations and Controlled Teleportation Fidelity under Noisy Channels
summary: In distributed quantum computing, quantum networks provide a potential infrastructure for long-range quantum information processing. Controlled quantum teleportation (CQT) is a key practically relevant protocol that can connect two parties on a network and enables a third party, the controller to allow or abort the secure teleportation of an arbitrary single-qubit state between the two parties. We investigate the robustness of a three-qubit GHZ resource under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise. Using the Kraus-operator formalism, we characterize the noisy resource through multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC), localizable entanglement (LE), and CQT fidelity. We also outline a proof-of-concept photonic implementation for preparing the three-qubit GHZ resource and realizing the CQT protocol, which could enable experimental investigation of the effects of noise. Our results show that bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise generally preserve useful mutipartite quantum correlations over broader noise parameter ranges. Interestingly, multipartite discord exhibits freezing under bit-flip noise over a finite parameter regime. Moreover, discord can persist beyond the sudden death of genuine multipartite entanglement, revealing the distinct robustness of nonclassical correlations. We further demonstrate that CQT fidelity which characterizes the performance of CQT can exceed the classical threshold even after GMC vanishes, while LE more closely reflects the operational usefulness of the noisy resource. These findings highlight the complementary roles of quantum correlations and entanglement in assessing the resilience of GHZ-based protocols.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how a three-qubit GHZ resource for controlled quantum teleportation (CQT) degrades under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise, characterized via multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence, localizable entanglement, and CQT fidelity, with a proof-of-concept photonic implementation outlined.
AI.motivation: Distributed quantum computing and quantum networks require robust long-range protocols; CQT is a key candidate connecting two parties via a third-party controller, but its resilience to realistic noise on the GHZ resource is unclear. The work aims to quantify the robustness and operational usefulness of the noisy GHZ resource.
AI.method: Noise channels (bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, amplitude-damping) are modeled with the Kraus-operator formalism applied to a three-qubit GHZ state. The noisy resource is characterized by multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC), localizable entanglement (LE), and CQT fidelity. A proof-of-concept photonic scheme for preparing the GHZ resource and realizing CQT is outlined.
AI.result: Bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise sustain useful multipartite correlations over wider noise-parameter ranges. Multipartite discord exhibits freezing under bit-flip noise in a finite regime, and discord persists beyond the sudden death of GMC. CQT fidelity can exceed the classical threshold even after GMC vanishes, while LE tracks operational usefulness more faithfully.
AI.conclusion: Quantum correlations and entanglement play complementary roles in assessing GHZ-based protocol resilience; discord-type correlations offer robustness advantages, and LE better reflects operational usefulness than GMC for CQT performance under noise.

title: Real-space construction and selection rules of center-of-mass momentum eigenstates in two-dimensional many-body lattices
summary: We present a comprehensive framework for the real-space construction of center-of-mass (c.m.) momentum eigenstates in two-dimensional (2D) quantum many-body systems. Unlike standard momentum-space approaches, our real-space formalism explicitly captures the non-uniformity of cyclic subspace dimensions, which are fundamentally governed by the spatial symmetries of the many-body configurations and particle statistics. We demonstrate that performing 2D real-space translations on multi-particle states naturally induces non-trivial translation phase factors associated with the characters of these stabilizer subgroups, leading to a renormalization of permissible momentum values. Notably, we identify an anomalous cross-dimensional momentum coupling in highly symmetric particle distributions, where the permissible momentum values in one direction are strictly constrained by those in the perpendicular direction. We emphasize the algorithmic necessity of this coupling, as neglecting it leads to missing or duplicated basis states in numerical implementations. Concrete examples are provided to demonstrate the practical implementation and physical consequences of this framework.

AI.tldr: A real-space framework constructs center-of-mass momentum eigenstates for 2D quantum many-body systems, capturing non-uniform cyclic subspace dimensions and revealing symmetry-induced phase factors and an anomalous cross-dimensional momentum coupling between perpendicular directions.
AI.motivation: Standard momentum-space approaches do not explicitly capture the non-uniformity of cyclic subspace dimensions in 2D many-body systems, which depend on spatial symmetries and particle statistics. A real-space formalism is needed to properly account for these effects.
AI.method: The authors build c.m. momentum eigenstates directly in real space. They analyze 2D real-space translations on multi-particle states, derive the translation phase factors tied to characters of stabilizer subgroups, and use these to renormalize the admissible momentum quantum numbers.
AI.result: Translation phases renormalize permissible momentum values. In highly symmetric particle distributions, an anomalous cross-dimensional momentum coupling emerges, where permissible momenta in one direction constrain those in the perpendicular direction; omitting it causes missing or duplicated basis states. Concrete examples illustrate implementation and physical consequences.
AI.conclusion: Real-space construction provides a rigorous, algorithmically necessary treatment of c.m. momentum eigenstates in 2D many-body systems; the cross-dimensional momentum coupling must be included for correct, non-degenerate basis enumeration.

title: Quantum Cryptomania with Classical Communication without One-Way Functions
summary:
In classical cryptography, one-way functions are necessary for most of cryptography. In the quantum world, however, Kretschmer at {TQC'21} and subsequent works have demonstrated that quantum versions of various primitives in minicrypt, such as signatures and private-key encryption, do not require quantum-computable one-way functions (\textsf{qOWF}s). However, the question of the necessity of \textsf{qOWF}s for primitives in Cryptomania like public-key encryption with classical public keys and ciphertexts (\textsf{qPKE}) has remained open.
  We provide a comprehensive picture of the relationship between \textsf{qPKE} and \textsf{qOWF}. First, our main result is a black-box separation between \textsf{qOWF}s and \textsf{qPKE}. In particular, we show that relative to a unitary, real, and self-inverse oracle, there exists a \textsf{qPKE} scheme (with classical keys and ciphertexts), but \textsf{qOWF}s do not exist. Further, our oracles admit a point-function obfuscation construction, thus ruling out black-box construction of \textsf{qOWF} from point function obfuscations.
  On the positive side, we construct \textsf{qPKE} from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for quantum circuits with classical obfuscated descriptions and efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles, which is known to be a potentially weaker assumption than \textsf{qOWF}s, due to an existing black-box separation. Our construction is the quantum analog of the classical construction of \textsf{PKE} from one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation in the quantum computation with classical communication (QCCC) setting.

AI.tldr: The paper fully characterizes the relationship between quantum public-key encryption (qPKE with classical keys/ciphertexts) and quantum one-way functions (qOWF): it gives a black-box separation (in a real, self-inverse unitary oracle there is qPKE but no qOWF, also ruling out black-box qOWF from point-function obfuscation) and positive constructions of qPKE from quantum iO plus efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles.
AI.motivation: Kretschmer (TQC'21) and follow-ups showed that minicrypt primitives (signatures, private-key encryption) need not imply qOWFs in the quantum world, so the necessity of qOWFs for Cryptomania-level primitives, in particular public-key encryption with classical public keys and ciphertexts (qPKE), remained open.
AI.method: A black-box separation is shown by exhibiting a unitary, real, self-inverse oracle relative to which a qPKE scheme (classical keys and ciphertexts) exists while qOWFs do not; the oracle additionally supports a point-function obfuscation construction. For the positive direction, qPKE is built from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for quantum circuits with classical obfuscated descriptions together with efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles, translating the classical QCCC construction of PKE from OWF and iO.
AI.result: Relative to the constructed oracle, qPKE exists but qOWFs do not, which also rules out black-box constructions of qOWFs from point-function obfuscation. Conversely, qPKE is constructed from quantum iO plus efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles, assumptions separated from qOWFs by an existing black-box separation.
AI.conclusion: qOWFs are not necessary for qPKE in a black-box sense, yet qPKE remains achievable from plausibly weaker assumptions (quantum iO and efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles), providing a comprehensive picture of the qPKE–qOWF relationship.

title: Trident: Efficient Load Verification for Yoked Surface Codes using a Three-Level Memory Hierarchy
comment: 17 pages, 14 figures, to be published in Proceedings of the 32nd ACM International Conference on Architectural Support for Programming Languages and Operating Systems, Volume 1 (ASPLOS '27)
summary:
Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQCs) commonly use the surface code to encode program qubits as error-corrected logical qubits. Unfortunately, the surface code has a poor encoding rate, so recent work has proposed Yoked Surface Codes (YSCs), which concatenate the surface code with a high-rate quantum code. The surface code qubits in YSCs are protected by the checks, or yokes, of the high-rate code. YSCs have 1D and 2D variants, which are $1.8\times$ and $4.5\times$ more efficient than the surface code, respectively.
  Modern FTQC architectures use a two-level hierarchy: surface codes perform logical operations (compute) while 2D YSCs store idle program qubits (memory). To load a qubit from memory, the FTQC first performs retrieval, which logically moves a program qubit from a 2D YSC into a surface code (8 cycles). However, retrieval is not fault-tolerant, so the FTQC must verify the load by measuring all the yokes of the 2D YSC (178 cycles). As verification dominates memory access latency, eliminating it can provide a speedup of $5.7\times$.
  Our goal is to reduce the verification overhead of 2D YSCs while retaining their storage efficiency. We exploit the fact that 1D YSCs, though less storage-efficient, incur negligible verification latency. We propose Trident, which expands the two-level hierarchy into a three-level hierarchy by adding a small intermediate level containing a 1D YSC (L1). If most loads hit L1 rather than L2 (2D YSC tier), it can significantly reduce verification overhead. We present two variants: Trident-D (demand-driven) and Trident-P (prefetch-driven), which achieve speedups of $2.8\times$ and $4.2\times$, respectively, while increasing the physical qubit cost of memory by only 4.9%.

AI.tldr: Trident adds an intermediate 1D Yoked Surface Code tier between surface-code compute and 2D-YSC memory to eliminate costly fault-tolerance verification on memory loads, achieving up to 4.2x speedup at only 4.9% extra memory qubit cost.
AI.motivation: 2D Yoked Surface Codes are 4.5x more storage-efficient than surface codes, but loading a qubit requires a non-fault-tolerant retrieval (8 cycles) followed by a 178-cycle yoke-measurement verification, which dominates memory access latency; eliminating it could yield a 5.7x speedup.
AI.method: Extend the standard two-level (surface code compute / 2D YSC memory) hierarchy into a three-level hierarchy by inserting a small L1 tier of 1D YSCs, which have negligible verification latency despite lower storage efficiency, so most loads are served from L1 instead of L2. Two policies are proposed: Trident-D (demand-driven) and Trident-P (prefetch-driven).
AI.result: Trident-D achieves a 2.8x speedup and Trident-P a 4.2x speedup, while increasing memory's physical qubit cost by only 4.9%.
AI.conclusion: Inserting a lightweight 1D-YSC intermediate tier largely absorbs verification overhead in 2D-YSC-based memory hierarchies, retaining high storage efficiency with minimal qubit overhead; prefetch-driven placement outperforms demand-driven.

title: Photon-Number Discrimination from Increasing Time-of-Arrival Separation in Wide Superconducting Microstrip Single-Photon Detectors
summary: Measurements of photon-number-dependent time-of-arrival (TOA) distributions in wide NbN superconducting microstrip single-photon detectors (SMSPDs) are presented. Two \SI{10}{\um}-long devices with widths of \SI{3.2}{\um} and \SI{6.4}{\um} are characterized under pulsed \SI{515}{nm} excitation. The TOA histograms are described by sums of exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) components, with the wider device exhibiting components assigned to photon numbers up to \(n=8\). Adjacent TOA peaks become more distinguishable relative to their widths at higher photon number, in contrast to the compression of neighboring photon-number timing shifts observed in conventional narrow-wire SNSPDs. For the components assigned to \(n=7\) and \(n=8\), the FWHM-normalized peak separation is \(2.15\), and the fitted EMG distributions yield an equal-prior pairwise TOA-assignment fidelity of \(99.6\%\). The EMG exponential-tail parameter \(τ_n\) decreases strongly with photon number, while the Gaussian-location parameter \(μ_n\) continues to shift between neighboring components. A phenomenological model motivated by absorption-site-dependent vortex processes and collective current redistribution captures these timing trends. These results support wide SMSPDs as a platform for TOA-based photon-number discrimination at high photon number, relevant to multiphoton-state characterization and photonic quantum information processing. The same geometry also provides a setting to examine how the spatial distribution of photon absorption affects vortex-assisted detection.

AI.tldr: Photon-number-resolved time-of-arrival histograms in wide (3.2 and 6.4 µm) NbN superconducting microstrip single-photon detectors show resolvable peaks up to n=8, with 99.6% pairwise assignment fidelity at n=7 vs n=8.
AI.motivation: Conventional narrow-wire SNSPDs suffer compression of neighboring photon-number timing shifts, limiting time-of-arrival (TOA)-based photon-number discrimination at high photon number; wide superconducting microstrip detectors may circumvent this.
AI.method: Two 10-µm-long NbN SMSPDs (3.2 and 6.4 µm wide) under pulsed 515 nm excitation; TOA histograms fitted as sums of exponentially modified Gaussian (EMG) components assigned to photon numbers, plus a phenomenological model based on absorption-site-dependent vortex processes and collective current redistribution.
AI.result: The wider device resolves components up to n=8; adjacent TOA peaks become more distinguishable relative to their widths at higher n. For n=7 and n=8 the FWHM-normalized peak separation is 2.15, giving 99.6% equal-prior pairwise TOA-assignment fidelity. EMG tail parameter τn decreases strongly with photon number while μn continues to shift between neighboring components.
AI.conclusion: Wide SMSPDs enable TOA-based photon-number discrimination at high photon number, relevant to multiphoton-state characterization and photonic quantum information processing; the geometry also probes how absorption-site spatial distribution affects vortex-assisted detection.

title: Quantum Evolution Networks Learn Long-Time Coherent Dynamics in Driven Spin Registers
summary: Predicting and controlling driven quantum systems requires access to dynamics across physical parameters, initial states, and evolution times. A reusable neural model must capture this dependence while preserving unitary structure and maintaining accuracy over long-time coherent evolution. Here we introduce Quantum Evolution Networks (QENs), which map physical parameters and time to complete propagators for periodically driven three-spin registers. Shared networks learn unitary one-period propagators and compatible within-period paths, enabling predictions through known periodic composition without query-specific numerical integration. For transverse driving, the fifth-percentile fidelity, minimized over input states and sampled times, is 0.9947 over 24 periods on 256 held-out configurations. A leading-order analysis of spectrally resolved endpoint residuals predicts multicycle process error more accurately than quadratic or spectrum-averaged estimates. Interventions at matched single-period infidelity produce orders-of-magnitude differences in multicycle infidelity, demonstrating the importance of residual orientation. Compatible component replacements identify how endpoint and within-period approximations limit reconstruction accuracy. These results establish a reusable neural representation of the studied propagator families and connect its learned residual structure to its observed long-time reliability.

AI.tldr: Quantum Evolution Networks (QENs) learn reusable neural representations that map physical parameters and time to full propagators of periodically driven three-spin registers, achieving high long-time fidelity without query-specific numerical integration.
AI.motivation: Predicting and controlling driven quantum systems requires dynamics across many parameters, initial states, and times, while preserving unitary structure and accuracy over long-time coherent evolution—goals not met by per-query numerical integration.
AI.method: QENs use shared networks to learn unitary one-period propagators plus compatible within-period paths, then predict arbitrary times via known periodic composition. A leading-order analysis of spectrally resolved endpoint residuals is used to predict multicycle process error, and matched-infidelity interventions plus compatible component replacements probe error structure.
AI.result: For transverse driving, fifth-percentile fidelity (minimized over input states and sampled times) is 0.9947 over 24 periods on 256 held-out configurations. The leading-order residual analysis predicts multicycle error better than quadratic or spectrum-averaged estimates; matched single-period infidelity interventions yield orders-of-magnitude differences in multicycle infidelity.
AI.conclusion: QENs provide a reusable neural representation of the studied propagator families, and their learned residual structure—particularly residual orientation—explains long-time reliability.

title: Bogoliubov Dynamics and Zitterbewegung in Optical Dirac Systems
summary: We develop a bosonic Bogoliubov description of Zitterbewegung in time-dependent optical-Dirac systems. Within the optical-Dirac framework, the anomalous pair-creation and pair-annihilation terms of a bosonic Bogoliubov Hamiltonian correspond to couplings between the positive- and negative-frequency sectors, whose coherence underlies the Zitterbewegung response. When the constitutive parameters vary in time, the resulting moving-frame connection generates dynamical interbranch coupling and positive--negative-frequency coherence. Under periodic modulation, this coupling becomes resonant near $Ω\simeq2ω_0$, leading to parametric amplification of the coherence and consequently to an enhanced Zitterbewegung motion.

AI.tldr: A bosonic Bogoliubov framework describes Zitterbewegung in time-dependent optical-Dirac systems, where anomalous pair terms couple positive/negative-frequency sectors; periodic modulation at Ω≈2ω₀ resonantly amplifies this coherence and enhances the Zitterbewegung motion.
AI.motivation: To provide a systematic bosonic Bogoliubov description of Zitterbewegung (ZB) in optical-Dirac systems, and to understand how time-varying constitutive parameters dynamically generate and control the interbranch coupling that drives the ZB response.
AI.method: The authors model the optical-Dirac system with a bosonic Bogoliubov Hamiltonian whose anomalous pair-creation/annihilation terms represent couplings between positive- and negative-frequency sectors. Time-dependent constitutive parameters induce a moving-frame connection that generates dynamical interbranch coupling and positive–negative-frequency coherence. Periodic modulation is then analyzed near the resonance condition Ω ≃ 2ω₀.
AI.result: The positive–negative-frequency coherence underlies the ZB response. Under periodic modulation, the dynamically generated coupling becomes resonant near Ω ≃ 2ω₀, producing parametric amplification of the coherence and a corresponding enhanced ZB motion.
AI.conclusion: Zitterbewegung in optical-Dirac systems can be understood and actively controlled via a bosonic Bogoliubov picture: resonant periodic modulation (Ω ≃ 2ω₀) parametrically amplifies interbranch coherence, offering a route to enhanced and tunable ZB dynamics.

title: Traceable Quantum Secret Sharing
summary: Quantum secret sharing protects distributed quantum information against unauthorized reconstruction, yet existing schemes provide no intrinsic accountability when shares are leaked or forged. This missing capability is particularly relevant in realistic distributed settings, where compromised participants may either expose valid shares or maliciously interfere with reconstruction. Here we establish a framework for traceable quantum secret sharing under these two threat models. We introduce leakage-verifiable and traceable quantum secret sharing (LVT-QSS), which attributes leaked shares through an explicit leakage verification mechanism, and malicious-traceable and accountable quantum secret sharing (MTA-QSS), which identifies participants who submit forged shares during reconstruction. We formulate security definitions for both settings and prove that the proposed protocols satisfy the corresponding guarantees against the relevant adversaries. Numerical simulations under per-share depolarizing noise further quantify the robustness of the proposed schemes and identify verification as the dominant noise sensitive stage. These results incorporate accountability into quantum secret sharing and provide a foundation for traceable distributed quantum cryptography.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a framework for traceable quantum secret sharing with accountability under two threat models: leakage-verifiable and traceable QSS (LVT-QSS) for attributing leaked shares, and malicious-traceable accountable QSS (MTA-QSS) for identifying forgers during reconstruction, with formal security definitions, proofs, and noise simulations.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum secret sharing schemes provide no intrinsic accountability when shares are leaked or forged, a critical gap in realistic distributed settings where compromised participants may expose valid shares or maliciously interfere with reconstruction.
AI.method: Proposes two protocols: LVT-QSS with an explicit leakage verification mechanism to attribute leaked shares, and MTA-QSS to identify participants submitting forged shares during reconstruction. Formal security definitions are formulated for both settings, with proofs of the corresponding guarantees against relevant adversaries, plus numerical simulations under per-share depolarizing noise.
AI.result: The proposed protocols are proven to satisfy the corresponding security guarantees against the relevant adversaries under both threat models. Numerical simulations under per-share depolarizing noise quantify robustness and identify the verification stage as the dominant noise-sensitive stage.
AI.conclusion: The work incorporates accountability into quantum secret sharing, establishing traceable quantum secret sharing as a foundation for traceable distributed quantum cryptography.

title: Performing a Quantum Subroutine Using Cluster States
summary: Quantum subroutines, like their classical counterparts, serve as essential components of larger algorithms. They can be realized using gate based architectures or measurement based quantum computation (MBQC), where computation proceeds through adaptive measurements on highly entangled cluster states. In this work, we implement a phase oracle as a reusable subroutine within the MBQC framework using experimentally feasible cluster states.
