Unlike prior demonstrations of Grover's algorithm in MBQC that omit explicit oracle construction, our approach provides a transparent formulation of the oracle subroutine, including its measurement patterns, byproduct correlations, density-matrix simulations, and corresponding MBQC measurement circuits.

AI.tldr: This work implements a reusable phase oracle subroutine within measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) using experimentally feasible cluster states, providing an explicit construction with measurement patterns, byproduct correlations, density-matrix simulations, and MBQC measurement circuits.
AI.motivation: Prior MBQC demonstrations of Grover's algorithm omit explicit oracle construction, leaving the oracle subroutine opaque; the authors aim to formulate this essential component transparently within the MBQC framework.
AI.method: The phase oracle is realized as a measurement-based subroutine on cluster states, characterized via measurement patterns, byproduct correlations, density-matrix simulations, and corresponding MBQC measurement circuits, designed in a way compatible with feasible experimental cluster states.
AI.result: The authors provide a complete and explicit MBQC description of the phase oracle subroutine, including its measurement patterns, byproduct dependencies, and validated density-matrix simulations, contrasting with earlier Grover-on-MBQC demonstrations that lacked explicit oracle formulation.
AI.conclusion: Explicit, reusable oracle subroutines can be constructed and validated in MBQC, enabling transparent and experimentally realistic realizations of larger measurement-based quantum algorithms such as Grover's search.

title: Two-Layer Verification for Fault-Tolerant Magic-State Preparation in High-Rate Quantum Codes
summary: Encoded magic states are essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their resource-efficient preparation in high-rate quantum codes remains challenging. To address this limitation, we propose two-layer verification, which combines local verification of independently prepared subblocks with logical verification after their embedding into a target code. This hierarchy detects harmful error patterns, including even-parity logical-eigenvalue flips that are invisible to a collective product check alone. We demonstrate this scheme for a $[[21,3,5]]$ code by constructing a circuit that embeds three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into the target code. Circuit-level simulations of $T$- and $S$-state preparation show logical-error suppression consistent with the code distance. These results demonstrate the potential of two-layer verification as a design principle for reliable magic-state preparation in quantum codes encoding multiple logical qubits.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes "two-layer verification" to prepare encoded magic states reliably in high-rate quantum codes, combining per-subblock verification with logical verification after embedding, and demonstrates it for a $[[21,3,5]]$ code.
AI.motivation: Encoded magic states are required for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, yet preparing them resource-efficiently in high-rate codes is difficult; existing collective product checks miss harmful even-parity logical-eigenvalue flips.
AI.method: Two-layer verification: local verification of independently prepared subblocks plus logical verification after embedding into the target code. Demonstrated with a circuit that embeds three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into a $[[21,3,5]]$ code.
AI.result: Circuit-level simulations of $T$- and $S$-state preparation show logical-error suppression consistent with the code distance.
AI.conclusion: Two-layer verification is a viable design principle for reliable magic-state preparation in quantum codes encoding multiple logical qubits.

title: Near-field maps of topological edge states of molecular aggregates
summary: Self-assembled two-dimensional molecular aggregates provide a versatile platform for engineering excitonic states, including topologically nontrivial edge states. However, these edge-states are difficult to probe optically: they have weak far-field transition strengths, and far-field spectra do not reveal whether an excitation is localized at the edge. For an aggregate consisting of two sublattices of molecules with genuinely complex transition dipoles, we show that spatially resolved near-field spectroscopy encodes the full spatial structure of these states. The resulting near-field maps do not mirror the site populations, but instead exhibit strongly nonuniform, interference-like features. We demonstrate that a convolutional neural network can reconstruct the complex expansion coefficients of the eigenstates from these maps, and that this reconstruction is robust against substantial random noise.

AI.tldr: Spatially resolved near-field spectroscopy combined with a convolutional neural network reconstructs the complex eigenstate expansion coefficients of edge states in two-sublattice molecular aggregates with complex transition dipoles, and does so robustly under substantial noise.
AI.motivation: Topologically nontrivial edge states in self-assembled 2D molecular aggregates are hard to probe optically: their far-field transition strengths are weak, and far-field spectra cannot reveal whether an excitation is localized at the edge.
AI.method: Analyze an aggregate with two sublattices of molecules possessing genuinely complex transition dipoles; compute spatially resolved near-field maps of the excitonic eigenstates, and train a convolutional neural network to invert these maps into the complex expansion coefficients of the eigenstates.
AI.result: Near-field maps do not mirror site populations but show strongly nonuniform, interference-like features encoding full spatial structure; the CNN reconstructs the complex eigenstate coefficients from these maps and remains robust against substantial random noise.
AI.conclusion: Spatially resolved near-field spectroscopy provides a viable route to optically accessing and characterizing topologically nontrivial edge states in molecular aggregates, with learned inversion enabling full eigenstate reconstruction despite noise.

title: High Resolution Hyperspectral Quantum Infrared Imaging with Undetected Photons
summary: Quantum sensing in the infrared regime often demands the use of expensive and cryogenically operated detectors. Nonlinear interferometry has paved the way for information transfer from the infrared to the near--infrared or visible regime in various quantum technologies. A particularly interesting application of these interferometers involves spectrally--resolved quantum imaging using undetected photons, enabled by the use of temperature--tunable parametric amplifiers. In this work, we demonstrate spectrally resolved transmission imaging with undetected photons around 1550 nm using a spontaneous parametric down conversion based folded nonlinear interferometric scheme, registering the attenuation of a zebrafish larva as a biological feasibility test. We characterize and calibrate the interferometer, having achieved spectrally resolved interference fringes with a maximum baseline visibility of $\sim 74\%$ in the near--infrared regime. Phase--stepped readout of a grating spectrometer gives a resolving power of $\sim1460$ (from the spectrometer's point spread function) at 1550 nm, and $\sim 730$ from the coherence length, the finest reported for imaging with undetected photons, over an instantaneous spectral window of $\approx 51$ cm$^{-1}$.

AI.tldr: Demonstrates spectrally resolved transmission imaging with undetected photons near 1550 nm using a folded nonlinear interferometer with temperature-tunable parametric amplifiers, achieving high spectral resolution and a biological feasibility test on a zebrafish larva.
AI.motivation: Infrared quantum sensing typically requires expensive, cryogenically cooled detectors. Nonlinear interferometry enables transferring information from the infrared to the near-infrared/visible, but spectrally resolved imaging with undetected photons needs improved spectral resolution and practical biological validation.
AI.method: A spontaneous parametric down-conversion (SPDC)-based folded nonlinear interferometric scheme with temperature-tunable parametric amplifiers; phase-stepped readout of a grating spectrometer is used to perform spectrally resolved transmission imaging with undetected photons around 1550 nm.
AI.result: Achieved spectrally resolved interference fringes with maximum baseline visibility of ~74% in the near-infrared; a resolving power of ~1460 (from the spectrometer point spread function) and ~730 (from the coherence length) at 1550 nm over an instantaneous spectral window of ~51 cm^-1—the finest reported for imaging with undetected photons. The attenuation of a zebrafish larva was registered as a biological feasibility test.
AI.conclusion: The folded nonlinear interferometer with temperature-tunable parametric amplifiers enables high-resolution spectrally resolved imaging with undetected photons at 1550 nm, offering a practical, detector-cost-reducing route for infrared quantum imaging with biological applicability.

title: Fundamental bound on Wigner negativity generation from environmental collisions
summary: Beyond quadratic potentials, classical evolution laws are typically thought to arise from quantum theory as an approximate description. Here we show that classical evolution laws can emerge exactly, provided the environment interacts with the system via collisions. We use this to derive an inequality that lower bounds the distribution of environmental momentum kicks by the absolute value of the Fourier transform of the potential. We show that violating this inequality is necessary and sufficient for a non-quadratic potential to generate negativity from the set of positive Wigner functions. A simple consequence of this is a lower bound on the heating rate for a quantum system to evolve effectively classically. We illustrate our results using the theory of a levitated nanoparticle subject to photon recoil and background gas collisions. We derive the strength of external potential needed to generate Wigner negative states in an optical tweezer and propose an experimental test of whether a nanoparticle in an optical lattice is operating in a non-classical regime.

AI.tldr: The authors prove that classical evolution laws can arise exactly (not just approximately) when the environment interacts with the system via collisions, and derive an inequality bounding environmental momentum-kick distributions by the Fourier transform of the potential, which is necessary and sufficient for non-quadratic potentials to create Wigner negativity.
AI.motivation: Standard wisdom holds that classical dynamics emerges from quantum theory only as an approximate description beyond quadratic potentials. The authors seek to identify exact conditions under which genuinely classical evolution is recovered, and to connect this to a physically measurable criterion (Wigner negativity generation).
AI.method: They model the environment as interacting with the system through collisions and derive an inequality that lower-bounds the distribution of environmental momentum kicks by the absolute value of the Fourier transform of the potential. They show that violating this inequality is necessary and sufficient for a non-quadratic potential to generate negativity from the set of positive Wigner functions. They apply the framework to a levitated nanoparticle subject to photon recoil and background gas collisions.
AI.result: The inequality yields a lower bound on the heating rate required for a quantum system to evolve effectively classically. For an optically levitated nanoparticle, they derive the external potential strength needed to generate Wigner-negative states in an optical tweezer, and propose an experimental test of whether a nanoparticle in an optical lattice operates in a non-classical regime.
AI.conclusion: Classical evolution can emerge exactly under collisional system-environment coupling, with the Fourier transform of the potential quantifying the momentum-kick threshold. The framework provides experimentally testable predictions for levitated nanoparticles in optical tweezers and lattices.

title: Finite Nonsignalling Resources Suffice to Simulate Entangled Qubits
summary: A longstanding question in Bell nonlocality is whether finite-alphabet nonsignalling resources can reproduce the continuum of measurement correlations of partially entangled qubits. Here we resolve this problem by showing that every fixed pure two-qubit state admits an exact simulation of all local projective-measurement statistics using shared randomness and finitely many Popescu-Rohrlich (PR) boxes, without communication or postselection. The boxes operate in parallel, with a worst-case bound independent of the measurement settings: at most $128\cot^4θ$ calls for the Schmidt state $\cosθ|00\rangle+\sinθ|11\rangle$, $0<θ<π/4$. The key is an exact finite-selection method that reduces input-dependent continuous sampling to a choice from a fixed-length shared random list, implemented through a finite PR-box network. The construction extends to arbitrary mixed two-qubit states and local binary-outcome POVMs. This reveals a fundamental separation between the continuity of quantum measurement correlations and the alphabet size of the resources needed to simulate them, shedding light on the resource-theoretic structure of Bell nonlocality.

AI.tldr: Every fixed pure two-qubit state can be exactly simulated with shared randomness and finitely many PR boxes operating in parallel, bounded by at most 128·cot^4 θ calls for the Schmidt state, with no communication or postselection.
AI.motivation: A longstanding question in Bell nonlocality: can finite-alphabet nonsignalling resources reproduce the continuum of measurement correlations of partially entangled qubits? Prior work left open whether exact (not approximate) simulation with finitely many PR boxes is possible for all local projective measurements on a fixed state.
AI.method: An exact finite-selection method converts input-dependent continuous sampling into selecting from a fixed-length shared random list, implemented via a finite PR-box network running in parallel.
AI.result: Exact simulation of all local projective-measurement statistics for every fixed pure two-qubit state, using shared randomness plus finitely many PR boxes with a worst-case, setting-independent bound of at most 128·cot^4 θ calls for cosθ|00⟩+sinθ|11⟩ (0<θ<π/4). The construction extends to arbitrary mixed two-qubit states and local binary-outcome POVMs.
AI.conclusion: There is a fundamental separation between the continuity of quantum measurement correlations and the alphabet size of resources needed to simulate them, clarifying the resource-theoretic structure of Bell nonlocality.

title: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
summary: We demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations using \texttt{ibm\_phoenix}, a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits that are capable of fast reset. Using strategies to exclude underperforming components together with noise informed decoding, we routinely produce surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with logical error per round below 1\%. We demonstrate entanglement between two logical qubits, where logical Bell-state fidelities above 93\% are observed for entanglement created via lattice surgery. With three logical qubits and lattice surgery, we perform logical teleportation of a range of states and gates, observing fidelities in the range 78\% - 93\%. Using reset to reduce qubit leakage, we show that repeated rounds of stabilizer measurements continue to exhibit improvements in a stability experiment up to $\sim 2\cdot 10^{-7}$ over 170 measurement rounds.

AI.tldr: High-fidelity logical qubit operations on a 120-qubit superconducting device achieve surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with sub-1% logical error per round, logical Bell-state fidelities above 93%, logical teleportation at 78%-93%, and improved stability over 170 rounds.
AI.motivation: To show that practical quantum error correction (surface codes) with fault-tolerant logical operations can be realized at useful fidelities on a large superconducting qubit array, motivating scalable logical-qubit computation.
AI.method: Uses ibm_phoenix, a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits with fast reset. Employs component-selection strategies that exclude underperforming qubits and noise-informed (noise-aware) decoding. Implements surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5, forms entanglement between two logical qubits via lattice surgery, performs logical teleportation with three logical qubits, and uses reset to reduce qubit leakage in repeated stabilizer measurement rounds.
AI.result: Distance-3 and distance-5 surface codes routinely achieve logical error per round below 1%. Logical Bell-state fidelities above 93% are observed for lattice-surgery entanglement. Logical teleportation across a range of states and gates yields fidelities of 78%-93%. In a stability experiment up to ~2·10^-7 over 170 measurement rounds, resetting to reduce leakage sustains improvements in repeated stabilizer measurement rounds.
AI.conclusion: These results demonstrate that large superconducting arrays with fast reset, combined with component selection and noise-informed decoding, can support high-fidelity surface-code logical qubits and multi-logical-qubit operations (entanglement, teleportation), with leakage mitigation via reset enabling stable, extended repeated syndrome measurement—advancing toward fault-tolerant logical computation.

title: Quantum theory of laser noise in coherent-scattering levitated optomechanics
summary: State purity is a key resource for experimental tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects. Cavity cooling of a levitated nanoparticle via coherent scattering stands out as a strategy to prepare highly pure states of its roto-translational motion. In several cases, though, the performance of cooling by coherent scattering is limited by the classical fluctuations of the laser field. Here we present a quantum theory of coherent-scattering experiments which includes the effect of the laser amplitude and phase noise. We derive a master equation for the noise-averaged particle's dynamics, valid for both center-of-mass and rotational degrees of freedom, and quantify the cooling performance for different levels of noise in state-of-the-art experiments. We compute approximate analytical expressions for the laser-noise-induced heating rates and excess phonon number in both regimes of weak and strong optomechanical coupling. Moreover, our model can be applied to laser noise processes with generic power spectral densities and finite correlation times. This work offers a toolbox to quantify and optimize the state purity in coherent-scattering experiments, and opens new avenues towards the preparation of quantum states with levitated systems.

AI.tldr: A quantum theory of cavity cooling via coherent scattering that incorporates laser amplitude and phase noise, providing a master equation and analytical heating-rate expressions to quantify state purity in levitated-nanoparticle experiments.
AI.motivation: Cavity cooling of levitated nanoparticles via coherent scattering is a leading route to prepare highly pure roto-translational states for tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects, but its performance is degraded by classical laser field fluctuations. A quantitative framework accounting for laser noise was missing.
AI.method: Develops a quantum theory of coherent-scattering experiments including laser amplitude and phase noise. Derives a master equation for the noise-averaged particle dynamics valid for both center-of-mass and rotational degrees of freedom, and computes approximate analytical expressions for laser-noise-induced heating rates and excess phonon number in the weak and strong optomechanical coupling regimes. The model handles noise processes with generic power spectral densities and finite correlation times.
AI.result: Quantifies cooling performance for different noise levels in state-of-the-art experiments, yielding analytical formulas for noise-induced heating rates and excess phonon occupation in both coupling regimes, applicable to arbitrary noise spectra and finite correlation times.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a toolbox to quantify and optimize state purity in coherent-scattering experiments and opens avenues toward preparing quantum states with levitated systems.

title: Quantum Secret Sharing from CSS qLDPC Codes: Computable Access Structures, Accessible Logical Dimension, and Topology-Aware Network Cost
comment: 34 pages with the appendix starting at page 26
summary: Quantum secret sharing (QSS) schemes can be constructed from quantum error-correcting codes, but characterizing their access structures and implementation costs becomes challenging for finite-length, high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. We develop an exact computational framework for QSS induced by CSS qLDPC codes. The framework characterizes authorized, forbidden, and intermediate coalitions using restricted parity-check matrices and binary linear algebra, and introduces the accessible logical dimension \(κ(A)\), defined through the symplectic rank of locally supported logical classes, to refine the characterization of intermediate coalitions. We further incorporate physical network constraints through separate Tanner-incidence, Steiner-routing, and scheduling-depth costs, and treat the partitioning of physical qubits into participants as an explicit design variable. Numerical experiments on four CSS qLDPC codes verify the predicted complement duality and monotonicity properties and show substantial variation in access transitions and network costs. For the codes studied, the bivariate bicycle instance exhibits the sharpest transition, while network embedding costs vary by more than an order of magnitude across physical topologies. We also show that participant partitioning can substantially improve block-level security and reconstruction thresholds. These results provide a practical bridge between the algebraic structure of CSS qLDPC codes, the graded accessibility of quantum secrets, and the physical constraints of networked QSS implementations.

AI.tldr: An exact computational framework characterizes access structures and implementation costs of quantum secret sharing built from finite-length CSS qLDPC codes, introducing an accessible logical dimension and explicit physical-network costs.
AI.motivation: QSS can be built from quantum error-correcting codes, but for finite-length, high-rate qLDPC codes the access structure and implementation cost are hard to characterize.
AI.method: Uses restricted parity-check matrices and binary linear algebra to classify authorized, forbidden, and intermediate coalitions; defines accessible logical dimension κ(A) via symplectic rank of locally supported logical classes; models physical costs as Tanner-incidence, Steiner-routing, and scheduling-depth terms; treats qubit-to-participant partitioning as a design variable.
AI.result: Experiments on four CSS qLDPC codes confirm predicted complement duality and monotonicity; access transitions and network costs vary widely; the bivariate bicycle instance shows the sharpest transition; embedding costs differ by over an order of magnitude across topologies; partitioning improves block-level security and reconstruction thresholds.
AI.conclusion: The framework links CSS qLDPC algebraic structure, graded secret accessibility, and physical network constraints, offering a practical tool for designing networked QSS implementations.

title: LYNX - A trapped-ion quantum information processor
summary: We introduce LYNX, a quantum information processor based on trapped $^{40}$Ca$^+$ ions. It utilizes up to 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity. We characterize the system performance using rigorous benchmarks, such as randomized benchmarking (RB), GHZ state fidelity estimates, and quantum volume (QV) tests. The LYNX processor shows average 1-qubit gate errors of $8(5)\times 10^{-5}$ tested via standard RB in a 24-qubit register. An average 2-qubit gate error in a 24-qubit register of $2.84(8)\times 10^{-3}$ is demonstrated using interleaved RB. Furthermore, the device passes QV tests using up to 15 qubits which corresponds to a quantum volume of QV$=2^{15}$.

AI.tldr: LYNX is a trapped-ion quantum processor with up to 31 all-to-all connected qubits, benchmarked via RB, GHZ fidelity, and quantum volume, achieving 1Q and 2Q gate errors of ~8e-5 and ~2.84e-3 respectively, and QV=2^15.
AI.motivation: To present and characterize a trapped-ion quantum information processor platform, demonstrating its scalability and performance under rigorous, standardized benchmarks.
AI.method: A trapped-40Ca+ ion system supporting up to 31 qubits with all-to-all connectivity, evaluated by randomized benchmarking (standard and interleaved), GHZ state fidelity estimation, and quantum volume tests in registers up to 24 qubits.
AI.result: Average 1-qubit gate error 8(5)e-5 (standard RB, 24 qubits); average 2-qubit gate error 2.84(8)e-3 (interleaved RB, 24 qubits); passes QV tests up to 15 qubits, giving QV=2^15.
AI.conclusion: The LYNX processor demonstrates competitive fidelities and verified quantum volume, establishing it as a capable trapped-ion platform with all-to-all connectivity for multi-qubit applications.

title: Photon-Pair Advantage for Dissipative Parameter Estimation in Whispering-Gallery-Mode Interferometers
summary: We study the estimation of detuning and intrinsic loss in a lossy whispering-gallery-mode (WGM) resonator located in a balanced Mach--Zehnder interferometer. We use indistinguishable photon pairs and coherent-state probes. We show that using indistinguishable photon pairs can provide higher Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) of dissipative parameters, such as intrinsic loss, at resonance away from critical coupling. Taking into account all photon-loss outcomes, we obtain analytical QFI expressions and compare photon-pair and coherent-state probe results when they have the same mean photon number. For estimating the round-trip amplitude transmission at resonance and away from critical coupling, the photon-pair probe gives a higher QFI than the coherent-state probe, and photon-number-resolved detection saturates this QFI. This advantage is due to the photon-loss statistics and it is still accessible for a typical overcoupled condition after averaging over fluctuations of the unresolved detuning. We identify the limits of this advantage: phase doubling does not improve resonant detuning estimation, and coincidence-only detection is inefficient close to a zero transmission. These results identify the cases in which photon pairs can be useful for absorption and pump--probe WGM sensing.

AI.tldr: Indistinguishable photon-pair probes outperform coherent states in Quantum Fisher Information for estimating intrinsic loss of a lossy WGM resonator in a balanced Mach-Zehnder interferometer, away from critical coupling at resonance, with photon-number-resolved detection saturating the bound.
AI.motivation: To determine whether quantum probes (indistinguishable photon pairs) can enhance sensing of dissipative parameters such as intrinsic loss and detuning in lossy whispering-gallery-mode resonators, and to establish the precise conditions and limits under which such an advantage exists relative to classical coherent-state probes at equal mean photon number.
AI.method: Model a lossy WGM resonator embedded in a balanced Mach-Zehnder interferometer probed by indistinguishable photon pairs and by coherent states. Compute analytical Quantum Fisher Information expressions for dissipative parameters (detuning, intrinsic loss, round-trip amplitude transmission), accounting for all photon-loss outcomes, and compare photon-pair versus coherent-state performance at equal mean photon number. Evaluate detection strategies (photon-number-resolved vs coincidence-only) and robustness to unresolved detuning fluctuations.
AI.result: Photon pairs yield higher QFI for intrinsic loss at resonance away from critical coupling. For round-trip amplitude transmission at resonance away from critical coupling, photon pairs give higher QFI than coherent states, and photon-number-resolved detection saturates this QFI. The advantage stems from photon-loss statistics and persists for typical overcoupled conditions after averaging over unresolved detuning fluctuations. Limits: phase doubling does not improve resonant detuning estimation, and coincidence-only detection is inefficient near zero transmission.
AI.conclusion: Photon pairs are beneficial quantum probes for absorption and pump-probe WGM sensing, but only in specific regimes (resonance, away from critical coupling, with number-resolved detection and surviving detuning fluctuations); the advantage does not extend to resonant detuning estimation via phase doubling nor to coincidence-only detection near zero transmission.

title: Classical Pre-Training of Large Shallow Parametrized Quantum Circuits through Pauli Propagation and deployment on Quantum Hardware
summary: Scaling parametrized quantum circuits to a larger number of qubits is a central challenge in Quantum Machine Learning: gradient estimation via the parameter-shift rule quickly becomes prohibitively expensive, while gradient-free optimizers offer limited convergence guarantees. We apply the Pauli propagation framework to a broad class of Quantum Machine Learning problems in which the loss is expressed as a function of expectation values of the circuit's observables, while keeping the relevant quantity of interest, such as the quantum state or its samples, classically intractable to compute. By propagating the observables backward through the circuit, we obtain an explicit parametric expression for the loss that can be minimized entirely on classical hardware. We also present complementary strategies to make propagation tractable at large scale, including weight-based and degree-based truncations and pruning heuristics. We demonstrate the approach on two benchmarks run on 64-qubit circuits: Variational Quantum Eigensolver on a two-dimensional Ising model, and training of a discrete-type generative model for binary images. In both cases, the classically pre-trained parameters are deployed on the IBM quantum processor ibm_berlin. For generative learning, we additionally show that the circuits considered here require substantially fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style ansätze, reducing transpilation overhead and making deployment on current quantum hardware feasible.

AI.tldr: The authors apply Pauli propagation to QML problems whose loss depends on observable expectation values, obtaining a classically tractable parametric loss for 64-qubit circuits, with truncation/pruning strategies and hardware deployment on ibm_berlin.
AI.motivation: Scaling parametrized quantum circuits to many qubits is hindered because parameter-shift gradient estimation becomes prohibitively expensive, while gradient-free optimizers offer weak convergence guarantees.
AI.method: Propagate observables backward through the circuit under the Pauli propagation framework to derive an explicit parametric expression of the loss minimizable entirely on classical hardware, supplemented by weight-based and degree-based truncations and pruning heuristics to keep propagation tractable at scale.
AI.result: Demonstrated on 64-qubit circuits for VQE on a two-dimensional Ising model and training of a discrete-type generative model for binary images; classically pre-trained parameters were deployed on ibm_berlin, and the generative circuits required substantially fewer parametrized gates than IQP-style ansätze, reducing transpilation overhead.
AI.conclusion: Pauli propagation enables classically optimizing large-scale QML losses while retaining classically intractable state/sample quantities, and the reduced gate counts make deployment on current quantum hardware feasible.

title: A note on the monotonicity of observational ergotropic advantage
comment: 7 pages, comments and suggestions are welcome
summary: Very recently, Mahanti et al. (arXiv:2609.18735) introduced the observational ergotropic advantage, which gives the maximum value of extra work that a measurement can obtain with respect to all incoherent measurements. However, the above quantity does not show monotonic behaviour under the resource theory of measurement coherence. So, the search for a resource theory in which it is a monotone was open. We derive the monotonicity of this quantity using energy-preserving channels and passive resets as free operations and energy-incoherent measurements as free objects. We show the monotonicity property of the measure as a necessary criterion of measurement transformation, but it turns out not to be a sufficient condition. It is further established that the measure is not convex. A short analysis of bounds and tightness of the measure using a degenerate Hamiltonian is also given.

AI.tldr: The paper shows that the observational ergotropic advantage is monotone under a resource theory with energy-preserving channels and passive resets as free operations and energy-incoherent measurements as free objects, but it is not convex and monotonicity is necessary yet not sufficient for measurement transformations.
AI.motivation: Mahanti et al. introduced the observational ergotropic advantage, the maximum extra work a measurement yields over all incoherent measurements, but it fails to be monotone under the resource theory of measurement coherence, leaving open the question of which resource theory makes it a genuine monotone.
AI.method: The authors construct a resource theory whose free operations are energy-preserving channels and passive resets, and whose free objects are energy-incoherent measurements, then derive the monotonicity of the observational ergotropic advantage in that framework and analyze it as a criterion for measurement transformation along with its convexity and bounds.
AI.result: The measure is shown to be monotone under the proposed free operations; monotonicity is a necessary but not sufficient criterion for measurement transformation; the measure is not convex; bounds and tightness are examined using a degenerate Hamiltonian.
AI.conclusion: The observational ergotropic advantage becomes a legitimate monotone in the resource theory based on energy-preserving channels, passive resets, and energy-incoherent measurements, though it is incomplete as a full characterization of state/measurement convertibility and lacks convexity.

title: The Compendium of Super-Quadratic Computational Quantum Advantages
summary: This compendium presents a structured collection of computational problems with credible prospects for realizing meaningful quantum advantage, focused on describing problem characteristics rather than specific algorithms. It is intended for non-quantum researchers and practitioners with strong computational backgrounds, particularly domain experts, seeking to assess the relevance of quantum methods to real-world problems. The compendium focuses on enumerating core problems for which there is good evidence that a quantum computer can realize more than a quadratic speedup in offline non-relativized time-complexity (e.g., as opposed to in oracular settings, streaming models, or communication advantages). Entries characterize the structural constraints that real-world instances must satisfy to realize those advantages in practice. The intention is to provide a reference that can be leveraged to connect quantum algorithms to practical use cases.

AI.tldr: A structured compendium of computational problems with credible prospects for meaningful (beyond-quadratic) quantum advantage, described by problem characteristics rather than specific algorithms, aimed at non-quantum domain experts to assess relevance to real-world problems.
AI.motivation: Non-quantum researchers and practitioners with strong computational backgrounds (especially domain experts) need a way to assess whether quantum methods are relevant to their real-world problems, but existing resources focus on algorithms rather than problem characteristics. There is a need for a reference that connects quantum algorithms to practical use cases by emphasizing the structural features of problems that enable quantum advantage.
AI.method: The authors assemble a structured collection (compendium) of core computational problems selected for good evidence of more than a quadratic speedup in offline, non-relativized time complexity—explicitly excluding oracular settings, streaming models, and communication advantages. Each entry characterizes the structural constraints that real-world instances must satisfy to realize the advantage, and the problems are described in terms of their characteristics rather than specific algorithms.
AI.result: A curated set of problem entries, each documenting the problem's characteristics and the structural constraints required for genuine quantum advantage in practice, enabling domain experts to map quantum algorithms to concrete use cases.
AI.conclusion: The compendium serves as a reference linking quantum algorithms to practical applications, targeting non-quantum practitioners and focusing on problem characteristics and real-world structural constraints rather than algorithm specifics.

title: QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems
summary:
We present QuantumBilliards.jl, an open-source Julia library providing a suite of numerical solvers for the two-dimensional interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, a paradigmatic model in quantum chaos. The library implements conventional wavenumber-sweep techniques together with several accelerated eigensolvers: the Vergini--Saraceno scaling method, the expanded boundary integral method (EBIM), Beyn's contour-integral method, and the Compact Rational Krylov (CORK) method. It provides a common framework for constructing billiard geometries, exploiting discrete symmetries, computing eigenvalues and eigenstates, and treating smooth, cornered, and multiply connected domains. The library further includes reconstruction of eigenfunctions from boundary normal derivatives and the computation of Poincaré--Husimi (PH) phase-space representations.
  Available at: https://github.com/Quantum-Chaos-Julia/QuantumBilliards.jl.

AI.tldr: QuantumBilliards.jl is an open-source Julia library for solving the 2D interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions, offering multiple conventional and accelerated eigensolvers within a unified framework.
AI.motivation: The 2D interior Helmholtz eigenproblem with Dirichlet boundary conditions is a paradigmatic model in quantum chaos, yet practical numerical work requires varied solvers, geometry handling, symmetry exploitation, and post-processing tools; a common library lowers the barrier to applying and comparing these methods.
AI.method: The library implements wavenumber-sweep techniques plus accelerated eigensolvers: the Vergini–Saraceno scaling method, the expanded boundary integral method (EBIM), Beyn's contour-integral method, and the Compact Rational Krylov (CORK) method. It provides a shared framework for constructing billiard geometries, exploiting discrete symmetries, computing eigenvalues and eigenstates, handling smooth/cornered/multiply connected domains, reconstructing eigenfunctions from boundary normal derivatives, and computing Poincaré–Husimi phase-space representations.
AI.result: A unified open-source Julia package offering both conventional and accelerated eigensolvers together with geometry construction, symmetry reduction, eigenfunction reconstruction, and phase-space representation tools, released at the given GitHub repository.
AI.conclusion: QuantumBilliards.jl consolidates multiple eigensolver strategies and supporting analysis tools for quantum billiards into one accessible, reusable framework.

title: Optimizing Quantum Battery via Counterdiabatic driving
summary: We analyze the energy charging of a quantum battery within an open quantum framework, where the interaction between the battery element and an external power source is mediated by an ancilla system acting as a controllable switch. Specifically, we investigate the charging and discharging dynamics of a cavity-based quantum battery coupled to a driven qubit functioning as the charger. To ensure lossless power transfer, we utilize an adiabatic evolution protocol. Furthermore, we implement counterdiabatic driving, achieved by applying an auxiliary control field to the original Hamiltonian, to suppress undesired transitions and realize fast adiabatic dynamics. This scheme significantly accelerates the charging process. We demonstrate that the charging efficiency under adiabatic evolution is enhanced and exhibits stable, non-oscillatory behavior, and we determine the optimal duration for the operation. Finally, we show that counterdiabatic driving minimizes the path length between the initial and final states, inducing the shortest possible evolution distance.

AI.tldr: Counterdiabatic driving of an ancilla-mediated charger accelerates lossless charging of a cavity-based quantum battery, enhancing efficiency and minimizing the evolution path length.
AI.motivation: Lossless, fast energy transfer from an external power source to a quantum battery is limited by undesired transitions and slow adiabatic protocols; the authors seek a controllable, accelerated charging scheme that preserves efficiency.
AI.method: Open-quantum-framework analysis of a cavity-based quantum battery coupled to a driven qubit charger, with an ancilla acting as a controllable switch. An adiabatic evolution protocol ensures lossless power transfer, and counterdiabatic driving via an auxiliary control field added to the original Hamiltonian suppresses unwanted transitions. Charging/discharging dynamics, charging efficiency, optimal operation duration, and state-space path length are evaluated.
AI.result: Counterdiabatic driving substantially accelerates charging while the adiabatic-evolution charging efficiency is enhanced and shows stable, non-oscillatory behavior; an optimal operation duration is identified. Counterdiabatic driving also minimizes the path length between initial and final states, yielding the shortest possible evolution distance.
AI.conclusion: Combining adiabatic protocols with counterdiabatic driving provides fast, efficient, and stable quantum battery charging, with path-length minimization as a useful figure of merit for optimal control of open quantum batteries.

title: Trace-distance characterization of recurrent pairwise synchronization in cavity-coupled superconducting qubits
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures. Submitted to Quantum Information Processing
summary: We theoretically investigate recurrent pairwise synchronization in three super?conducting qubits coupled to a common single-mode microwave cavity. The qubits interact indirectly through the cavity field and are driven by a coher?ent microwave field. We obtain the coherent dynamics in the dressed-state basis and quantify pairwise synchronization by the trace distance between reduced single-qubit density matrices. The trace-distance dynamics exhibit oscillatory wave-packet structures, with low-trace-distance regions identifying finite syn?chronization windows. An envelope-threshold procedure is introduced to extract the representative duration of these windows. By varying the middle-qubit coupling strength and the relative coupling ratio of the outer qubits, we con?struct a parameter-dependent map of the synchronization-window duration. The duration decreases rapidly with increasing relative outer-qubit coupling and becomes weakly dependent on the middle-qubit coupling in the stronger-coupling regime. These results provide a reduced-state-based characterization of coherent collective dynamics in multiqubit circuit-QED systems.

AI.tldr: The paper theoretically studies recurrent pairwise synchronization among three superconducting qubits coupled to a common single-mode cavity and driven by a coherent field, quantifying synchronization via the trace distance between reduced single-qubit density matrices and mapping synchronization-window durations across coupling parameters.
AI.motivation: Pairwise synchronization in multiqubit circuit-QED systems lacks a reduced-state-based characterization that captures coherent collective dynamics. The authors aim to quantify and map recurrent synchronization windows in a three-qubit common-cavity architecture.
AI.method: They model three superconducting qubits coupled to a common single-mode microwave cavity with a coherent drive, derive coherent dynamics in the dressed-state basis, and use the trace distance between reduced single-qubit density matrices to quantify pairwise synchronization. An envelope-threshold procedure extracts representative synchronization-window durations, which are mapped as a function of the middle-qubit coupling strength and the relative outer-qubit coupling ratio.
AI.result: Trace-distance dynamics show oscillatory wave-packet structures with low-trace-distance regions identifying finite synchronization windows. The synchronization-window duration decreases rapidly with increasing relative outer-qubit coupling and becomes only weakly dependent on middle-qubit coupling in the strong-coupling regime.
AI.conclusion: The trace-distance, envelope-threshold framework provides a reduced-state-based characterization of coherent collective synchronization dynamics in multiqubit circuit-QED systems and yields a parameter map of synchronization-window durations.

title: From Link Availability to Deadline-Constrained Key Service: A Feasibility Framework for Mobile Free-Space Quantum Key Distribution
summary: Mobile free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) links can provide secret bits intermittently, whereas applications may need cryptographic key material at specified times. Optical feasibility, positive finite-key output, and deadline-compliant key service are consequently different claims. This technical note formalizes their separation through a time-indexed, security-qualified arrival process and a key-inventory model. Under explicitly stated assumptions, an elementary prefix-feasibility condition characterizes whether all demands can be served without borrowing keys from future contact windows. A stylized finite block model then illustrates why positive long-run optical availability does not ensure positive finite-key output when observations are fragmented into short contacts. Two transparent numerical examples distinguish total key yield from key delivery time and show the conditional benefit of pooling data across acquisition windows. The analysis is intended as a systems-level accounting and benchmarking framework, not a new QKD security proof or a demonstration of hardware performance. It identifies measurements and security assumptions needed to evaluate train, UAV, high-altitude-platform, and satellite-assisted optical QKD against application-level service requirements.

AI.tldr: This technical note separates three distinct claims in mobile free-space QKD—optical feasibility, positive finite-key output, and deadline-compliant key service—using a time-indexed, security-qualified arrival process and key-inventory model, and shows via a stylized finite-block model that positive long-run optical availability does not guarantee positive finite-key output under fragmented short contacts.
AI.motivation: Mobile free-space QKD provides secret bits only intermittently, while applications require key material at specified times. Prior work conflates optical feasibility with actual finite-key output and with deadline-compliant service; these are logically different claims that need explicit separation and a systems-level accounting framework.
AI.method: Formalizes a time-indexed, security-qualified arrival process and a key-inventory model under explicitly stated assumptions. Derives an elementary prefix-feasibility condition characterizing whether all demands can be served without borrowing keys from future contact windows. Introduces a stylized finite block model to analyze fragmentation of observations into short contacts, and presents two transparent numerical examples separating total key yield from key delivery time and examining data pooling across acquisition windows.
AI.result: The prefix-feasibility condition characterizes deadline-compliant serviceability of all demands. The finite block model shows that positive long-run optical availability does not ensure positive finite-key output when observations are fragmented into short contacts. The numerical examples distinguish total key yield from key delivery time and demonstrate the conditional benefit of pooling data across acquisition windows.
AI.conclusion: The work is intended as a systems-level accounting and benchmarking framework rather than a new QKD security proof or hardware demonstration. It identifies the measurements and security assumptions required to evaluate train, UAV, high-altitude-platform, and satellite-assisted optical QKD against application-level service requirements.

title: An Invitation to Algebraic Methods in Quantum Theory
summary: In this paper, we present various well-studied examples of quantum systems, and discuss how they might be analysed algebraically. We analyse the harmonic oscillator, hydrogenic atom, optical components, and particle spin using multiple algebraic methods, and highlight the central importance of algebraic relationships between operators in determining the physical character of the system. In particular, we show: the ubiquity of the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(2,1)\cong\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$ as the ``spectrum generating algebra''; the role of $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ and $\mathfrak{su}(1,1)$ in determining the action of optical components; that an elementary algebraic approach to particle spin offers novel insights into its nature versus the usual approaches; and how understanding the full (often hidden) symmetry of a problem enables it to be solved immediately without the need to solve differential equations. We hope this work will serve as a gentle introduction to algebraic methods in quantum mechanics for the interested reader --- we therefore signpost active areas of research within the community.

AI.tldr: This pedagogical paper surveys algebraic methods for analysing well-studied quantum systems—harmonic oscillator, hydrogenic atom, optical components, and particle spin—emphasising how operator algebra relations determine physical character, and highlights the role of hidden symmetries in enabling immediate solutions without differential equations.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to provide a gentle, accessible introduction to algebraic methods in quantum mechanics for interested readers, and to signpost active research areas within the community.
AI.method: The paper analyses several quantum systems using multiple algebraic approaches, focusing on Lie algebras and algebraic relationships between operators. Specifically, it examines the ubiquity of the so(2,1) ≅ su(1,1) spectrum-generating algebra, the roles of su(2) and su(1,1) in optical component action, and an elementary algebraic treatment of particle spin.
AI.result: The paper demonstrates the central importance of operator algebraic relationships in determining the physical character of systems; shows the ubiquity of so(2,1) ≅ su(1,1) as a spectrum-generating algebra; clarifies the roles of su(2) and su(1,1) for optical components; offers novel insights into the nature of particle spin via an elementary algebraic approach compared to usual treatments; and illustrates how understanding full (often hidden) symmetries allows problems to be solved immediately without solving differential equations.
AI.conclusion: Algebraic methods offer a unifying and powerful framework for analysing quantum systems, with hidden symmetries enabling direct solutions. The work serves as a pedagogical introduction while identifying active research directions.

title: Elementary proofs of quantum lower bounds for element distinctness and k-sum
summary: We give elementary proofs of the $Ω(n^{2/3})$ quantum query lower bound for element distinctness and the $Ω(n^{k/(k+1)})$ lower bound for the $k$-sum problem, for fixed $k$ and sufficiently large groups. The proofs use only basic properties of quantum states and linear algebra, analyzing the differences of algorithm states on different inputs.

AI.tldr: Elementary proofs of the Ω(n^{2/3}) quantum query lower bound for element distinctness and the Ω(n^{k/(k+1)}) lower bound for k-sum, using only basic quantum-state and linear-algebra properties.
AI.motivation: Existing lower bounds for element distinctness and k-sum rely on heavier machinery (e.g., polynomial/adversary methods); the authors aim to provide simpler, self-contained, elementary proofs.
AI.method: Analyze the differences of algorithm states on different inputs, using only basic properties of quantum states and linear algebra, for fixed k and sufficiently large groups.
AI.result: Re-derive the Ω(n^{2/3}) lower bound for element distinctness and the Ω(n^{k/(k+1)}) lower bound for k-sum.
AI.conclusion: These fundamental quantum query lower bounds admit elementary, accessible proofs, clarifying the essential structure of the arguments.

title: Optimal probes for estimating the dephasing of a quantum spin system
summary: We investigate the optimal estimation of dephasing in finite-dimensional quantum spin systems. We first discuss some properties of the optimal probe states and present an efficient numerical algorithm to compute the optimal precision in dephasing estimation and identify the optimal probe states. For the dephasing channel arising from Gaussian phase diffusion, a spin cat state is known to be optimal for small dephasing. We analytically determine the range of dephasing strengths over which the cat state remains globally optimal for spins $J=1$ and $J=3/2$, and derive upper bounds on its optimality region for larger spins. We then compare numerically several probe states proposed in the literature, showing in particular that the simple class of probes obtained from uniform superpositions of all levels performs near-optimally for stronger dephasing. Finally, we apply our framework to a central-spin model coupled to a nuclear-spin bath, whose dynamics we simulate using the cluster-correlation expansion. Our results show that, while the cat state is optimal for weak Gaussian dephasing, pulse-controlled non-Markovian dynamics can favor states with amplitudes distributed over multiple spin levels, and in some cases the uniform state outperforms the other fixed probes considered. This shows how the choice of probe state depends both on the dephasing strength and on the dynamics.

AI.tldr: The paper studies optimal probe states for estimating dephasing in finite-dimensional quantum spin systems, provides a numerical algorithm for optimal precision, analytically bounds the optimality region of spin cat states, and compares alternative probes, including application to a central-spin nuclear-bath model.
AI.motivation: Dephasing estimation in spin systems is practically important, but the optimal probe states and their range of validity are only partially understood, particularly beyond the weak-dephasing regime and under realistic non-Markovian dynamics.
AI.method: The authors analyze properties of optimal probe states and develop an efficient numerical algorithm to compute optimal estimation precision and identify optimal probes. They analytically determine the dephasing-strength range where spin cat states remain globally optimal for J=1 and J=3/2, derive upper bounds for larger spins, numerically benchmark literature probe states (including uniform superpositions of all levels), and simulate a central-spin model coupled to a nuclear-spin bath via cluster-correlation expansion.
AI.result: Cat states are confirmed globally optimal over a determined range of Gaussian dephasing strengths for small spins, with upper bounds established for larger spins; uniform superposition probes perform near-optimally at stronger dephasing. Under pulse-controlled non-Markovian dynamics, states with amplitudes spread over multiple spin levels can be favored, and the uniform state sometimes outperforms other fixed probes.
AI.conclusion: The optimal probe choice depends on both dephasing strength and the underlying dynamics; cat states suit weak Gaussian dephasing, whereas stronger or non-Markovian regimes favor multi-level distributed states such as uniform superpositions.

title: Entanglement Asymmetry and Asymmetry Contour under Boundary Symmetry Breaking
summary: We investigate how symmetry-breaking boundary magnetic fields affect magnetization and Rényi-2 entanglement asymmetry (EA) in the transverse-field Ising model. For the ground state, magnetization exhibits qualitatively distinct behaviors in the ordered and disordered phases. EA also exhibits phase-dependent behavior, which is well captured by the lower and upper bounds derived in this work. In the critical regime, both magnetization and EA exhibit behavior qualitatively consistent with the field-theoretical predictions for a related setup. We also study boundary-quench dynamics and find that magnetization propagates from the boundary into the bulk with a velocity consistent with the maximum quasiparticle velocity. In contrast, because EA is a subsystem-integrated quantity, its spatial structure is not directly resolved. We therefore introduce the asymmetry contour, a contour-like finite-difference quantity that provides a spatially resolved characterization of the symmetry-breaking information encoded in the reduced density matrix. The resulting contour is complementary to the local magnetization, retaining sensitivity to nonlocal many-body correlations while its dynamics also reflects the underlying quasiparticle propagation. These results show how EA and its contour can provide complementary information-theoretic characterizations of symmetry breaking and its spatial structure.

AI.tldr: Symmetry-breaking boundary fields produce phase-dependent magnetization and Rényi-2 entanglement asymmetry (EA) in the transverse-field Ising model; a new "asymmetry contour" quantity spatially resolves symmetry-breaking information encoded in the reduced density matrix and tracks quasiparticle propagation after a boundary quench.
AI.motivation: The paper aims to clarify how symmetry-breaking boundary magnetic fields influence both local observables (magnetization) and information-theoretic quantities (Rényi-2 entanglement asymmetry) across the ordered, disordered, and critical phases, and to overcome the fact that EA, being a subsystem-integrated quantity, lacks direct spatial resolution.
AI.method: Study of the transverse-field Ising model with symmetry-breaking boundary magnetic fields: analysis of ground-state magnetization and Rényi-2 EA against derived lower/upper bounds and field-theoretical predictions; study of boundary-quench dynamics; introduction of the "asymmetry contour," a contour-like finite-difference quantity giving spatially resolved characterization of symmetry-breaking information in the reduced density matrix.
AI.result: Ground-state magnetization shows qualitatively distinct behavior in ordered vs. disordered phases; EA is phase-dependent and well captured by the derived bounds; in the critical regime both quantities agree qualitatively with field-theory predictions. Under boundary quench, magnetization propagates from boundary into bulk at a velocity consistent with the maximum quasiparticle velocity. The asymmetry contour is complementary to local magnetization, retaining sensitivity to nonlocal many-body correlations while its dynamics reflects quasiparticle propagation.
AI.conclusion: EA and its contour provide complementary information-theoretic characterizations of symmetry breaking and its spatial structure, linking local magnetization, nonlocal correlations, and quasiparticle dynamics.

title: Quantum Machine Learning in Medical Imaging: A Primer for Radiologists
summary: Deep learning has transformed radiology, but the computational cost of training and deploying modern models is outpacing what classical hardware can support. Quantum computing has been proposed as one response to this bottleneck: an n-qubit system can represent $2^n$ states simultaneously, although practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone. This review introduces radiologists to five core quantum concepts, qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, and quantum circuits, and to the superconducting, trapped-ion, and photonic hardware platforms that define the current noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) era. We then summarize the quantum machine learning architectures most often applied to medical imaging (quantum support vector machines, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, and quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations such as the flexible representation of quantum images (FRQI) and the novel enhanced quantum representation (NEQR). Reported applications include brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. Nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible. We conclude with current limitations and translational priorities for radiology.

AI.tldr: A tutorial-style review that introduces radiologists to qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates and circuits, NISQ hardware, and quantum ML/image representations, then surveys early medical imaging applications (tumor classification, pneumonia detection, lesion classification, CT/PET reconstruction, ultrasound denoising), concluding that nearly all work is small-scale hybrid quantum-classical research not yet ready for clinical deployment.
AI.motivation: Deep learning has transformed radiology, but training and deploying modern models imposes computational costs that classical hardware can no longer sustain. Quantum computing is proposed as a potential response to this bottleneck, yet radiologists generally lack the background to evaluate quantum claims, and practical speedups require efficient algorithms, data encoding, and measurement strategies rather than superposition alone.
AI.method: A narrative/tutorial review aimed at a radiology audience. It pedagogically introduces five core quantum concepts (qubits, superposition, entanglement, quantum gates, quantum circuits) and the three leading NISQ hardware platforms (superconducting, trapped-ion, photonic). It then surveys quantum machine learning architectures commonly applied to medical imaging (quantum SVM, quantum neural networks, variational quantum circuits, quantum convolutional neural networks) and quantum image representations (FRQI, NEQR), organizing reported applications across modalities such as MRI, chest radiography, dermatology/mammography, CT, PET, and ultrasound.
AI.result: Reported applications span brain tumor classification and segmentation on MRI, pneumonia detection on chest radiographs, skin and breast lesion classification, CT and PET reconstruction, and ultrasound denoising. However, nearly all published systems are hybrid quantum-classical pipelines evaluated only on small, downsampled benchmark datasets or simulators, and clinical deployment is not yet feasible.
AI.conclusion: Quantum computing for medical imaging remains at an early, proof-of-concept stage. The review closes by articulating current limitations (hardware scale and noise, data encoding, measurement overhead, dataset size, lack of clinical validation) and translational priorities for radiology, framing quantum advantages as unproven until demonstrated through rigorous, clinically relevant benchmarking.

title: Bounding single-copy information causality violations
summary: Information causality is a physical principle that constrains bipartite post-quantum nonlocal correlations from information-theoretic assumptions. A direct characterization of the correlations satisfying it, however, remains difficult because the defining entropic condition must hold for all admissible protocols in the corresponding task. Here, we formulate the single-copy information causality problem as an optimization over all protocol parameters and simplify it by proving a deterministic reduction. We then show that generic adaptive multi-copy protocols can be represented as single-copy protocols applied to an effective behavior obtained by local wirings. As a consequence, for families of correlations closed under wirings, excluding single-copy violations suffices to exclude all finite-copy adaptive-protocol violations. We formulate the resulting membership and set-inclusion problems as optimization problems and discuss possible semidefinite programming relaxations. As an application, we study expansions of the information causality functional around zero-capacity channels, generalizing a method recently employed by Gachechiladze and Miklin to derive the Tsirelson--Landau--Masanes boundary from information causality. For expansions centered on channels whose output distribution has full support, imposing the second-order constraints for all single-copy protocols characterizes exactly the set of macroscopic locality in the CHSH scenario. Expanding instead around appropriate constant-output channels with perturbations that change the channel support, we show that every single-copy IC violation can be witnessed already at first order with a channel of arbitrarily small capacity.

AI.tldr: The paper reformulates single-copy information causality (IC) as an optimization problem, proves a deterministic reduction, and shows adaptive multi-copy protocols reduce to single-copy protocols on wiring-derived effective behaviors, so excluding single-copy violations suffices for wiring-closed families. Using local expansions around zero-capacity channels, it recovers macroscopic locality in the CHSH scenario at second order and shows single-copy IC violations are first-order witnessable with arbitrarily small channel capacity.
AI.motivation: IC is a key information-theoretic principle bounding post-quantum bipartite nonlocal correlations, but directly characterizing the correlations that satisfy it is hard: the defining entropic inequality must hold across all admissible protocols in the corresponding task. The paper aims to make IC membership tractable and to connect single-copy constraints to multi-copy adaptive ones.
AI.method: Single-copy IC is cast as an optimization over all protocol parameters and simplified via a proven deterministic reduction. Generic adaptive multi-copy protocols are shown to be representable as single-copy protocols applied to an effective behavior produced by local wirings. The resulting membership and set-inclusion problems are then formulated as optimizations admitting SDP relaxations. Expansions of the IC functional around zero-capacity channels are analyzed: second-order constraints at full-support output distributions, and first-order perturbations around constant-output channels that alter support.
AI.result: For families closed under wirings, excluding single-copy IC violations suffices to rule out all finite-copy adaptive-protocol violations. Around full-support channels, imposing second-order single-copy constraints exactly characterizes macroscopic locality in the CHSH scenario, generalizing the Gachechiladze–Miklin derivation of the Tsirelson–Landau–Masanes boundary. Around support-changing constant-output channels, every single-copy IC violation is witnessed already at first order with a channel of arbitrarily small capacity.
AI.conclusion: Single-copy IC is sufficient to certify IC for wiring-closed correlation families, and local expansions of the IC functional provide a systematic route to characterizing physical correlation sets (e.g., macroscopic locality) and to detecting violations with minimal-capacity channels.

title: Exploiting the Weyl-Chamber Structure for Hardware-Aware Quantum Circuit Compression
summary: Quantum circuit compression based on tensor networks enables long-time simulation of quantum many-body dynamics on near-term hardware. While Riemannian optimization has been successfully employed for this purpose, it typically optimizes over the manifold of generic two-qubit unitaries. Consequently, the resulting gates must still be synthesized into the hardware's native gate set via KAK decomposition, an overhead that partially negates the original compression gain. We show that Riemannian-optimized gates already exhibit a predictable Weyl structure: near-$R_{ZZ}$ for the Ising model and near-fSim for the Heisenberg XXZ model. Building on this insight, we investigate whether parameterized optimization directly over the native gate set can offer a beneficial trade-off between expressivity and circuit efficiency by reducing the circuit's dimensionality. When comparing the two approaches, we find that the small residual Weyl parameters neglected by the latter are essential for high compression of the Ising propagator, whereas for the Heisenberg propagator, the native XXZ structure can be exploited directly to build a more efficient compressed circuit.

AI.tldr: The authors show that Riemannian-optimized compression gates have a predictable Weyl structure (near-R_ZZ for Ising, near-fSim for Heisenberg XXZ), and compare optimizing directly over hardware-native gate sets against generic two-qubit unitaries for quantum circuit compression.
AI.motivation: Riemannian optimization compresses circuits over the manifold of generic two-qubit unitaries, but the resulting gates must still be synthesized into the native gate set via KAK decomposition, an overhead that partially cancels the compression gain. The work asks whether restricting optimization to native gates yields a better expressivity/efficiency trade-off.
AI.method: Analyze the Weyl coordinates of Riemannian-optimized two-qubit gates for Ising and Heisenberg XXZ propagators, then investigate parameterized optimization directly over native gate sets with reduced dimensionality, comparing against the generic-unitary approach.
AI.result: Optimized gates concentrate near R_ZZ (Ising) and near fSim (Heisenberg XXZ) in Weyl space. For the Ising propagator, the small residual Weyl parameters dropped by native-set optimization are essential for high compression, so it performs worse; for the Heisenberg propagator, the native XXZ structure is exploited directly to build a more efficient compressed circuit.
AI.conclusion: Native gate-set optimization only pays off when the target dynamics aligns with the hardware's native structure (Heisenberg XXZ), while it loses compression for Ising where residual Weyl parameters matter—suggesting a structure-aware choice between the two approaches.

title: Minimal unitary representations of time-invariant causal quantum channels
summary: In this work, we study quantum channels that respect causality in single-input-single-output linear time-invariant systems. We show that positive semidefinite kernels satisfying certain analyticity constraints, which we call Schur-class kernels, provide a suitable description of such channels through multiplicative maps (Schur multipliers). Using the Moore-Aronszajn Theorem, we establish that these multipliers admit a minimal analytic Stinespring representation, which, in the unital case, is given by multiplication by a left inner function. We then relate the output rank of pure-state inputs to the dimension of the associated reproducing kernel Hilbert space. Using de Branges-Rovnyak realizations, we derive a stability criterion for the existence of two-sided inner completions of these vector-valued functions. We further show that the adjoint of the Julia embedding associated with the realization is minimal, and that its characteristic function essentially coincides with the canonical two-sided inner completion suggested by the Beurling-Lax-Halmos Theorem. Finally, we provide algorithms for explicitly computing minimal two-sided inner completions in the case of finite McMillan degree.

AI.tldr: The paper characterizes causality-respecting quantum channels in SISO LTI systems via Schur-class kernels and Schur multipliers, establishes a minimal analytic Stinespring representation, and derives a stability criterion for two-sided inner completions with explicit finite-degree algorithms.
AI.motivation: Quantum channels respecting causality in single-input-single-output linear time-invariant systems require a rigorous mathematical description. The authors aim to connect such channels to reproducing kernel Hilbert space theory and inner-function completions.
AI.method: Positive semidefinite Schur-class kernels satisfying analyticity constraints are used to describe the channels through multiplicative maps (Schur multipliers). The Moore-Aronszajn Theorem yields a minimal analytic Stinespring representation (multiplication by a left inner function in the unital case). Output rank of pure-state inputs is linked to the RKHS dimension. De Branges-Rovnyak realizations give a stability criterion for two-sided inner completions, and the Julia embedding adjoint is shown minimal, with characteristic function matching the canonical completion from the Beurling-Lax-Halmos Theorem. Algorithms compute minimal two-sided inner completions for finite McMillan degree.
AI.result: Schur-class kernels provide a suitable channel description; multipliers admit a minimal analytic Stinespring representation; the adjoint of the Julia embedding is minimal; its characteristic function essentially coincides with the canonical two-sided inner completion; explicit algorithms compute minimal completions in finite McMillan degree.
AI.conclusion: The work unifies quantum channel causality, reproducing kernel theory, and inner-function completion, providing both theoretical characterizations (Stinespring representation, stability criterion) and constructive algorithms for minimal two-sided inner completions.

title: Modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation via an interface between verified resources and online logical operations
summary: We introduce a factory--processor interface architecture for modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation that separates code-dependent encoded-resource preparation from reusable online logical processing on a common Gaussian optical processor. Beyond encoded resources, the interface specifies logical outputs, code-to-mode mapping, measurement roles, frame updates, verification records, and resource-injection boundaries. As a concrete realization, we combine an offline verified Bell-resource factory based on a recursively concatenated $C_4$ code with physical Gottesman--Kitaev--Preskill (GKP) qubits with an online time-domain measurement-based quantum computation (MBQC) processor. Under the specified additive-displacement-noise model and fixed postselection policy, simulations support the finite-level logical Bell-error ordering $P_5<P_4<P_3<P_2$ at 12.25 dB of effective GKP displacement-noise quality, both with and without the prescribed additional post-injection displacement noise. At 15.6 dB and $L=2$, a separate fixed-sample evaluation gives one-sided 95$\%$ Clopper--Pearson upper bounds below $10^{-5}$ for both conditions under the binomial model. The interface supports address-tracked injection, transversal CNOT and logical Bell-measurement constructions, and logical SWAP and Hadamard constructions with tracked code permutations. Given advance resource preparation and sufficient routing parallelism, increasing the concatenation level expands parallel encoded-resource width without increasing the protected online sequence length of these constructions. These results identify a modular route to lower logical error rates while retaining a common Gaussian MBQC operation set with shallow online processing.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a factory–processor interface for modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation that decouples code-dependent resource preparation from reusable online logical processing, and demonstrates a verified Bell-resource factory (recursively concatenated C4 code over GKP qubits) feeding a time-domain MBQC processor with favorable logical-error scaling and very low upper bounds.
AI.motivation: Modular optical fault-tolerant quantum computation needs a clean separation between code-specific resource preparation and reusable online logical processing on a common Gaussian optical platform; existing approaches entangle these concerns, complicating verification, scaling, and shallow online operation.
AI.method: Defines a factory–processor interface specifying logical outputs, code-to-mode mapping, measurement roles, frame updates, verification records, and resource-injection boundaries. Realizes it by combining an offline verified Bell-resource factory based on a recursively concatenated C4 code with physical GKP qubits, and an online time-domain MBQC processor. Evaluates under an additive-displacement-noise model with a fixed postselection policy, including prescribed additional post-injection displacement noise.
AI.result: Simulations support the finite-level logical Bell-error ordering P5<P4<P3<P2 at 12.25 dB effective GKP displacement-noise quality, with and without added post-injection noise. At 15.6 dB and L=2, a fixed-sample evaluation yields one-sided 95% Clopper–Pearson upper bounds below 1e-5 under a binomial model for both conditions. The interface supports address-tracked injection, transversal CNOT and logical Bell-measurement constructions, and logical SWAP and Hadamard with tracked code permutations.
AI.conclusion: Increasing the concatenation level expands parallel encoded-resource width without increasing the protected online sequence length (given advance resource preparation and sufficient routing parallelism). This identifies a modular route to lower logical error rates while retaining a common Gaussian MBQC operation set with shallow online processing.

title: Hardware-Friendly Estimation of LCU-Based Expectation Values via Quantum-to-Classical Workload Shifting
summary: Estimating the expectation value of an observable $O$ for a quantum state evolved under a general, possibly non-unitary, operator $A$ is a fundamental task in quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms. Existing linear-combination-of-unitaries (LCU) approaches implement $A$ on hardware, requiring ancilla qubits, controlled unitaries and, in randomized variants, fresh circuit executions for every Monte Carlo sample. These costs are prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices. We propose HERMES (Hardware-Efficient Reusable Measurements for Estimating LCU-based expectation valueS), which moves the processing of $A$ entirely to the classical domain.
