Expanding $A$ and $O$ in the Pauli basis and sampling pairs of Pauli terms classically, HERMES rewrites $μ= \mathrm{Tr}(OAρA^{\dagger})/\mathrm{Tr}(AρA^{\dagger})$ as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state $ρ$, with no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of $A$. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication and commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of the sample count, unlike randomized LCU methods whose circuit executions grow linearly with it. On ground-state energy estimation of $\mathrm{H}_2$ and $\mathrm{LiH}$ via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is also more robust to noise and completes a noisy $\mathrm{LiH}$ simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead growing with the number of Pauli terms in $A$.

AI.tldr: HERMES estimates observable expectation values for states evolved under a general non-unitary operator A by moving all processing of A to the classical domain, expanding A and O in the Pauli basis and classically sampling Pauli pairs, achieving measurement cost independent of sample count.
AI.motivation: Estimating Tr(OAρA†)/Tr(AρA†) for non-unitary A is fundamental to quantum simulation, chemistry, and variational algorithms, but existing LCU approaches require ancillas, controlled unitaries, and (in randomized variants) fresh circuit executions per Monte Carlo sample, which is prohibitive on NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices.
AI.method: HERMES expands A and O in the Pauli basis and classically samples pairs of Pauli terms, rewriting the target quantity as a ratio of weighted sums of Pauli expectation values on the unmodified state ρ — no ancillas, controlled unitaries, or quantum implementation of A. A two-level measurement reduction scheme (Pauli deduplication plus commuting-group partitioning) bounds the number of distinct measurement settings independently of sample count.
AI.result: On ground-state energy estimation of H2 and LiH via imaginary-time evolution, HERMES matches or beats a Pauli single-ancilla LCU baseline using shallow circuits with no two-qubit gates beyond state preparation under qubit-wise commuting grouping. It is more noise-robust and completes a noisy LiH simulation infeasible for the baseline, at the cost of classical overhead scaling with the number of Pauli terms in A.
AI.conclusion: HERMES offers a hardware-efficient, ancilla-free alternative to LCU for estimating LCU-based expectation values, trading classical overhead for reduced quantum resources and robustness, making it suitable for NISQ and early fault-tolerant devices.

title: Fermion Scattering on Quantum Computers
summary: Resonant scattering links particle interactions to the formation and decay of unstable excitations. We develop a hybrid quantum-computing framework to study these dynamics through fermion--antifermion collisions. Our formulation of $(1+1)$-dimensional Yukawa theory encodes fermions in qubits and the scalar field in qumodes. We identify the operations needed for a photonic implementation and benchmark the dynamics with tensor-network simulations. Near resonance, we resolve the build-up of a localised scalar excitation and the subsequent partial return of energy to the fermions. Enhanced entanglement accompanies this exchange. Time-dependent correlator measurements reproduce the analytically predicted decay rate to a few percent precision, with energy scans exhibiting a resonance peak consistent with packet-averaged Breit--Wigner behaviour. These results establish a concrete scattering benchmark for hybrid quantum computers and demonstrate how local real-time observables can probe particle-resonance dynamics.

AI.tldr: The authors introduce a hybrid quantum-computing framework (qubits for fermions, qumodes for the scalar field) to simulate fermion–antifermion collisions in (1+1)-dimensional Yukawa theory, benchmarking resonant scattering dynamics with tensor-network simulations.
AI.motivation: Resonant scattering connects particle interactions to the formation and decay of unstable excitations, but simulating this real-time dynamics is challenging; the work aims to establish quantum computing as a platform for such scattering problems.
AI.method: A hybrid qubit–qumode encoding of (1+1)D Yukawa theory: fermions mapped to qubits, the scalar field to qumodes. The required operations for a photonic implementation are identified, and the dynamics are benchmarked via tensor-network simulations, including time-dependent correlator measurements and energy scans.
AI.result: Near resonance, a localized scalar excitation builds up and energy partially returns to the fermions, accompanied by enhanced entanglement. Time-dependent correlators reproduce the analytic decay rate to a few percent precision, and energy scans show a resonance peak consistent with packet-averaged Breit–Wigner behavior.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a concrete scattering benchmark for hybrid quantum computers and show that local real-time observables can probe particle-resonance dynamics.

title: Nonclassicality from Incomplete Fock-State Statistics
comment: Main text: 7 pages, 5 figures; Supplemental Material: 22 pages, 12 figures
summary: Nonclassicality in bosonic systems can be certified directly from occupation probabilities without full state reconstruction. To complete a library of such criteria we introduce a numerical framework that constructs optimal linear nonclassicality witnesses from arbitrary subsets of measured occupation probabilities by solving a semi-infinite linear program. The method contains known analytical criteria as special cases while generally detecting substantially larger nonclassical regions. We provide an open-source implementation of the numerical optimization together with the analytical criteria discussed here, enabling direct application of the framework to measured occupation statistics across bosonic platforms. As a case study, we apply it to the resonant Jaynes--Cummings model with thermal states and reveal nonclassicality at short interaction times and close to thermal balance, where detection of nonclassicality is otherwise challenging.

AI.tldr: A semi-infinite linear program constructs optimal linear witnesses of bosonic nonclassicality directly from subsets of occupation probabilities, generalizing known analytical criteria and detecting larger nonclassical regions, with open-source code and a Jaynes–Cummings case study.
AI.motivation: Nonclassicality in bosonic systems is certifiable from occupation probabilities without full state reconstruction, but a complete library of such criteria is lacking; existing analytical criteria are limited and leave undetected nonclassical regions.
AI.method: Formulate the construction of optimal linear nonclassicality witnesses over arbitrary subsets of measured occupation probabilities as a semi-infinite linear program and solve it numerically; release open-source software including the analytical criteria; apply the framework to the resonant Jaynes–Cummings model with thermal states.
AI.result: Known analytical criteria emerge as special cases, while the numerical witnesses generally detect substantially larger nonclassical regions; in the thermal Jaynes–Cummings model nonclassicality is revealed at short interaction times and near thermal balance, where detection is otherwise difficult.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides a general, practically applicable tool for nonclassicality certification from measured occupation statistics across bosonic platforms, extendable via the open-source implementation.

title: One-sided-DIQKD using any pure bipartite entangled state secure against all attacks
summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) allows spatially separated parties to establish a secret key among themselves based on quantum principles. While QKD systems are being deployed worldwide, their reliance on trusted measurements makes them vulnerable. Moreover, existing protocols have largely focussed on the qubit cases, and rely on the maximally entangled state, a costly resource to generate. Here, we consider the one-sided-device-independent (1SDI) QKD protocols, where one of the measurement devices is trusted while the other is untrusted. The resource in this scenario is quantum steering, an asymmetric form of quantum nonlocality. This is inspired by a real-world scenario, where the trusted party can be considered to be a bank, or any large organisation that has sufficient resources to protect its systems and validate them, while the users are vulnerable to attacks. We then demonstrate that a secure key can be obtained using any pure bipartite entangled state in this setup. Considering realistic detectors and sources based on current technology, we demonstrate that even states that are almost separable can be used to extract a secure key. Moreover, for every pure entangled bipartite state, we find the critical detection efficiencies and visibility to obtain a secure key.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes one-sided-device-independent QKD protocols exploiting quantum steering, showing that any pure bipartite entangled state—even nearly separable ones—can yield a secure key under realistic detectors and sources, and derives critical detection efficiencies and visibilities for every pure entangled bipartite state.
AI.motivation: Existing QKD systems rely on trusted measurements, making them vulnerable, and most protocols focus on qubit cases requiring maximally entangled states, which are costly to generate. A real-world asymmetry exists where a resource-rich trusted party (e.g., a bank) interacts with vulnerable users, motivating a one-sided-device-independent approach based on quantum steering.
AI.method: Adopts a one-sided-device-independent (1SDI) QKD framework in which one measurement device is trusted (the resource-rich party) and the other untrusted, using quantum steering—an asymmetric form of quantum nonlocality—as the underlying resource. The analysis considers arbitrary pure bipartite entangled states and incorporates realistic detector and source models.
AI.result: A secure key can be obtained using any pure bipartite entangled state in this setup. With realistic detectors and sources, even states that are almost separable suffice to extract a secure key. For every pure entangled bipartite state, the critical detection efficiencies and visibility required for secure key extraction are identified.
AI.conclusion: Quantum steering enables practical, asymmetric 1SDI QKD that relaxes the need for maximally entangled states and tolerates imperfect, near-separable entanglement under realistic conditions, broadening the range of usable resources for secure key distribution.

title: Generating entanglement in quantum matter with pathway-entangled photons via resonant inelastic X-ray scattering
summary: Resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) is conventionally used to probe elementary excitations and correlations in quantum materials. Here, we propose an interferometric RIXS protocol that instead creates entanglement between spatially separated regions of a solid-state material. An incident X-ray photon is coherently split by a beam splitter into two arms illuminating opposite ends of a sample. Recombining the scattered photons at a second beam splitter and detecting an energy-selected photon then projects the material into a coherent superposition of excitations at the two ends. This protocol is the X-ray, solid-state analogue of the Duan-Lukin-Cirac-Zoller (DLCZ) heralding scheme. Using a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, we show that orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states. We illustrate this mechanism in three models: (1) two decoupled sites yield a heralded Bell state. (2) An open tight-binding chain exhibits reflection-parity-dependent interference, providing a benchmark for the interferometer's coherence. (3) A spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins. We also discuss practical considerations and challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.

AI.tldr: An interferometric RIXS protocol is proposed that uses a split X-ray photon recombined at a second beam splitter to herald entanglement between two spatially separated end regions of a solid-state sample, an X-ray analogue of DLCZ heralding.
AI.motivation: RIXS is conventionally a spectroscopic probe of elementary excitations; the authors aim to repurpose it as a tool that actively generates entanglement between distant regions of a quantum material, extending DLCZ-style heralded entanglement to X-ray, solid-state settings.
AI.method: An incident X-ray photon is coherently split into two arms illuminating opposite ends of the sample; scattered photons are recombined at a second beam splitter, and detection of an energy-selected photon projects the material into a coherent superposition of end excitations. The analysis uses a Kramers-Heisenberg formalism with quantized photon modes, illustrated with three models: two decoupled sites, an open tight-binding chain, and a spin-1 Haldane (AKLT) chain.
AI.result: Orthogonal and degenerate end excitations yield maximally entangled states; the two-site model gives a heralded Bell state, the open tight-binding chain shows reflection-parity-dependent interference serving as a coherence benchmark, and the AKLT chain yields an entangled pair of fractionalized edge spins.
AI.conclusion: Interferometric RIXS can herald maximally entangled states of separated end excitations, including fractionalized edge spins, and the paper discusses practical considerations and experimental challenges for realizing the protocol in X-ray experiments.

title: Certain Quantum States Already Require Quantum Time Evolution
summary: Model-independent tests of quantum theory, such as Bell inequality violations, focus on static properties of the theory and do not rely on its dynamical aspects. Hence, this core part of quantum theory remains largely untested in a model-independent way. We show that the structure of quantum time evolution can be examined by testing the consistency between the state space and the dynamical laws. Considering a class of generalized phase-space theories, we find that certain quantum states can only be part of a theory if the time evolution is quantum: their evolution in anharmonic potentials would otherwise result in unphysical, negative marginal distributions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the existence of the first excited state of a quantum harmonic oscillator is already sufficient to single out the Moyal bracket (quantum dynamics) to leading order in $\hbar^2$. We outline how theory-independent Wigner tomography of this state can be used to empirically exclude nonquantum dynamical theories.

AI.tldr: The authors propose model-independent tests of quantum dynamics by checking consistency between state space and time evolution in generalized phase-space theories, showing that certain quantum states require quantum dynamics and that the first excited harmonic-oscillator state already singles out the Moyal bracket to leading order in ℏ².
AI.motivation: Existing model-independent tests (e.g., Bell inequality violations) probe only static properties of quantum theory and leave its dynamical aspect—the structure of quantum time evolution—largely untested in a theory-independent manner.
AI.method: The authors test consistency between the state space and dynamical laws within a class of generalized phase-space theories. They analyze the evolution of certain quantum states in anharmonic potentials and examine whether nonquantum (non-Moyal) dynamics would produce unphysical negative marginal distributions. They also use the first excited state of a quantum harmonic oscillator and perform an expansion in ℏ² to identify which dynamics are compatible, outlining theory-independent Wigner tomography as an empirical protocol.
AI.result: Certain quantum states can belong to a theory only if time evolution is quantum; under nonquantum dynamics their evolution in anharmonic potentials yields unphysical negative marginal distributions. The existence of the first excited harmonic-oscillator state suffices to single out the Moyal bracket to leading order in ℏ².
AI.conclusion: Quantum time evolution can be examined model-independently via state-space/dynamics consistency, and theory-independent Wigner tomography of the first excited oscillator state offers an empirical route to exclude nonquantum dynamical theories.

title: Low-frustration block encodings by patch routing
summary: Block-encoding has emerged as a core primitive in many quantum algorithms, including quantum simulation. In this work, we design efficient and extensible methods for generating low-frustration block encodings of frustrated lattice Hamiltonians built from repeated local interaction patches through a technique we call "patch routing". We construct block encodings for a full Hamiltonian by first block-encoding a small local patch and then using a SWAP-style routing network to coherently apply the local patch encoding across the lattice. The expensive, local block-encoding cost is paid only once per query and is independent of lattice size, whereas the comparatively inexpensive routing network grows linearly with the lattice size, dominating at large sizes. Our method allows for a hierarchical structure in which larger patches can be block-encoded with small normalization factors, albeit at a higher (local, non-extensive) block-encoding cost, thereby reducing overall query complexity in an algorithm. We exploit symmetries and algebraic structures in local interactions to construct efficient block encodings, and we apply these techniques to the Heisenberg, Fermi-Hubbard, and honeycomb spin-liquid models. For a $120\times 120$ square-lattice $J_1$-$J_2$ Heisenberg model near maximal frustration ($J_2/J_1=0.4-0.6$), our methods result in a $15-17\times$ reduction in the leading $T$ cost per qubitized-QPE run (ignoring initial state preparation and overlap) relative to prior state-of-the-art Pauli LCU constructions. Corresponding reductions are approximately $3\times$ for the $120\times120$ Fermi-Hubbard model at half-filling. For time evolution of the honeycomb spin-liquid model on $120\times120$ unit cells, the leading cost is reduced by $5\times$. Our framework provides a systematic way forward for larger and more accurate fault-tolerant simulations of real-world quantum systems.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "patch routing," a method to build low-frustration block encodings of frustrated lattice Hamiltonians by encoding a small local interaction patch once and coherently replicating it across the lattice via a SWAP-style routing network, achieving significant query-complexity reductions for Heisenberg, Fermi-Hubbard, and honeycomb spin-liquid models.
AI.motivation: Block-encoding is a core primitive for quantum algorithms such as quantum simulation, but prior state-of-the-art constructions (e.g., Pauli LCU) suffer from large normalization factors and consequently high query complexity, especially for frustrated lattice Hamiltonians. There is a need for more efficient and extensible block-encoding methods that scale well with lattice size.
AI.method: The authors construct full-Hamiltonian block encodings in two stages: (1) block-encode a small local interaction patch once, independent of lattice size, and (2) apply this local encoding coherently across the lattice using an inexpensive SWAP-style routing network that scales linearly with lattice size. They support a hierarchical scheme where larger patches are encoded with small normalization factors at higher local (non-extensive) cost. Symmetries and algebraic structure of local interactions are exploited to build efficient local encodings, applied to Heisenberg, Fermi-Hubbard, and honeycomb spin-liquid models.
AI.result: For a 120×120 square-lattice J1-J2 Heisenberg model near maximal frustration (J2/J1 = 0.4–0.6), leading T cost per qubitized-QPE run is reduced 15–17× versus prior Pauli LCU constructions (excluding state prep and overlap). For the 120×120 half-filled Fermi-Hubbard model, reductions are ~3×; for honeycomb spin-liquid time evolution on 120×120 unit cells, the leading cost is reduced 5×.
AI.conclusion: Patch routing provides a systematic, extensible framework for generating low-frustration block encodings whose expensive local cost is paid once and is size-independent, while the linear-cost routing network dominates at large sizes. This enables larger and more accurate fault-tolerant simulations of real-world quantum systems.

title: Distributed Quantum-Centric Supercomputing with Multi-Layered Generative Learning for Intermolecular Interactions
summary: Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) approaches, such as sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD), combine quantum processors with high-performance computers (HPC), offering a promising route toward solving challenging electronic structure problems. However, implementation of QCSC approaches to large active space calculations is constrained by the associated number of qubits, deep quantum circuits, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a distributed QCSC framework that decomposes complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and reduced shot budgets. A physically motivated, two-step aggregation scheme then reconstructs the global solution: first, a computational bit assignment strategy optimizes a cost function to appropriately map local bit indices to global ones, yielding a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); second, an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restores missing cross-fragment interactions. Herein, we employ a multi-layered generative machine learning architecture, starting with utilizing the recently proposed physics-informed generative SQD (PIGen-SQD) as a distributed QCSC solver, followed by a secondary generative module to model configuration distributions and identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space. For water and formamide dimers, our method achieves up to $95\%$ reduction in the diagonalization dimension while enhancing energy accuracy by an order of magnitude over conventional SQD. Furthermore, application to the water hexamer ($\mathrm{(H_2O)_6}$) cage successfully decomposes a 120-qubit problem into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems, and stitches the monomers under a dimeric approximation, demonstrating excellent agreement with the reference classical methods.

AI.tldr: Distributed quantum-centric supercomputing framework that decomposes large active-space problems into parallel fragments solved by PIGen-SQD, then reconstructs global solutions via bit-assignment mapping and an inter-fragment correlation recovery generative module.
AI.motivation: Quantum-centric supercomputing (QCSC) and sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) can address challenging electronic structure problems, but scaling to large active spaces is limited by qubit count, circuit depth, sampling cost, and large-scale Hamiltonian diagonalization.
AI.method: A distributed QCSC framework splits complex molecular problems into parallel sub-problems requiring fewer qubits, shallower circuits, and smaller shot budgets. Global reconstruction uses a two-step aggregation scheme: (1) a computational bit assignment strategy that optimizes a cost function to map local bit indices to global ones, producing a mapped tensor product state (MTPS); (2) an inter-fragment correlation recovery module restoring missing cross-fragment interactions. The implementation uses a multi-layered generative ML architecture: PIGen-SQD as the distributed solver, followed by a secondary generative module modeling configuration distributions to identify dominant sectors of the global Hilbert space.
AI.result: For water and formamide dimers, up to 95% reduction in diagonalization dimension with an order-of-magnitude improvement in energy accuracy over conventional SQD. For the (H2O)6 cage, a 120-qubit problem is decomposed into six 20-qubit monomeric subsystems and stitched under a dimeric approximation, showing excellent agreement with reference classical methods.
AI.conclusion: Distributed QCSC with generative aggregation enables scalable, resource-efficient electronic structure calculations, demonstrating qubit reduction and accuracy gains, and successfully tackling a 120-qubit system through fragment decomposition.

title: Maximal Orbital Entanglement from Non-Interacting Fermions
summary: Orbital rotations are used in quantum many-body physics and chemistry to reduce the complexity of quantum states by compressing their correlation into a small set of relevant orbitals. In striking contrast, quantum information processing strives for the opposite: orbitals that maximize entanglement as a resource. Motivated by this, we prove that Slater determinants of $N$ fermions on a lattice of $d_A + d_B = d$ sites, although free of particle correlation, can carry up to $\min\{d_A, d_B, N, d-N\}$ ebits of orbital entanglement. Given enough particles and holes, this equals the maximum over all fermionic states. For arbitrary free states, we derive the maximal orbital total correlation in closed form for all bipartitions, the finest partition, and all partitions of up to five sites, using new majorization relations for Hermitian matrices. Taken together, these results turn mean-field states, the starting point of most many-body methods in physics and chemistry, into a viable resource for quantum information processing.

AI.tldr: Slater determinants, despite lacking particle correlations, can carry maximal orbital entanglement—up to min{d_A, d_B, N, d−N} ebits—making mean-field states a viable resource for quantum information.
AI.motivation: Orbital rotations compress correlations in many-body physics, but quantum information seeks the opposite: maximal entanglement. The authors aim to reconcile these opposing goals by quantifying orbital entanglement in free (mean-field) fermionic states.
AI.method: Analytical proof bounding orbital entanglement of Slater determinants of N fermions on d_A + d_B = d sites, plus derivation of closed-form maximal orbital total correlation for arbitrary free states across all bipartitions, the finest partition, and all partitions up to five sites, using new majorization relations for Hermitian matrices.
AI.result: Slater determinants can carry up to min{d_A, d_B, N, d−N} ebits of orbital entanglement; with sufficient particles and holes this saturates the maximum over all fermionic states. Closed-form maximal orbital total correlation is obtained for all bipartitions and the finest partition.
AI.conclusion: Mean-field states, the starting point of most many-body methods in physics and chemistry, are transformed into a viable resource for quantum information processing.
